11 Hardware Acceleration

Lecture slides for this chapter: Part 1 · Part 2

Purpose

Architecture stack focus for this chapter.

Why does moving data cost more than computing it?

Arithmetic is inexpensive relative to data movement. In the time required to fetch a single scalar operand from off-chip DRAM, modern arithmetic units can execute dozens to hundreds of floating-point operations, and that DRAM access consumes on the order of a hundred times more energy than the computation itself. This imbalance, the memory wall, means specialized accelerators are not merely faster arithmetic engines. Rather, their microarchitectures are designed to stage, amortize, and hide data movement through wide spatial interconnects, deep on-chip memory hierarchies, and specialized execution pipelines. When general-purpose processor scaling faltered, hardware specialization enabled machine learning models to continue scaling by turning transistor budgets into high-throughput tensor datapaths. Delivered performance, however, depends on whether a model’s tensor access patterns match the data paths of the underlying silicon. Hardware selection cannot be reduced to comparing peak FLOP/s: two accelerators with identical theoretical compute ratings often deliver radically different throughput on real workloads because one saturates its functional units while the other starves for data. A recommendation model dominated by sparse embedding lookups stresses memory bandwidth and interconnect latency, demanding a different memory architecture than a dense transformer training run bounded by matrix multiply-accumulate throughput. If an operation is bandwidth bound, reducing theoretical operation count yields zero speedup because arithmetic is not the binding constraint. Matching workload characteristics to architectural dataflows determines whether an accelerator operates near its hardware ceiling or languishes at a fraction of its advertised peak. In D·A·M terms, the accelerator makes the machine constraint concrete, governing which algorithms and model architectures remain practical in production.

Learning Objectives
  • Explain hardware acceleration as tensor-workload specialization and why Amdahl’s law bounds its end-to-end speedup
  • Compare Tensor Cores, systolic arrays, SIMD/SIMT units, and sparse execution for ML compute primitives
  • Diagnose memory-wall bottlenecks using bandwidth, cache hierarchy, host-device transfer, and energy-movement costs
  • Calculate arithmetic intensity and execution-path roofline ceilings, then use profiling to diagnose compute or memory limits
  • Select dataflow, tiling, and mapping strategies that maximize reuse under memory-capacity constraints
  • Analyze compiler and runtime optimizations that fuse kernels, plan memory, and schedule accelerators
  • Evaluate accelerator choices across throughput, latency, power, cost, and deployment-context constraints

11.1 Anatomy of an Accelerator

Hardware acceleration turns on the machine axis.

Model Compression closed on a deployment profile for ResNet-50 quantized to INT8 (ResNet-50 INT8 Deployment Profile on the Reference H100): a model four times smaller whose large-batch throughput rises severalfold on the reference H100 while its batch-one latency barely moves. Data selection reduced the iron law’s Data factor (\(\text{Samples/Task}\)) and compression reduced the Algorithm factor (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\)) and byte traffic (\(\DataVolume\)), but whether either saving reaches the wall clock is decided by the Machine factor (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)). This chapter supplies the machine side of that profile. It explains why the same INT8 weights run faster on one execution path than on another, and why the hardware, not the model, determines how much of every compression saving survives execution. The explanation starts with the memory wall: arithmetic is cheap relative to data movement, so specialized hardware matters less because it raises compute throughput than because it organizes memory, dataflow, and parallelism so that its arithmetic units stay fed.

One workload runs through the chapter. ResNet-50 quantized to INT8 carries the book’s compute-bound regime (Lighthouse Models as Reference Workloads): its convolutions reuse each weight across many image positions, so on a data-center accelerator most of its time can go to arithmetic rather than to moving bytes. It reappears at every level of the machine, from the matrix units that execute its convolutions to the compiler that lowers its graph, and each time the question is what the INT8 path changes. GPT-2 XL decoding one token at a time supplies the single contrast. It carries the bandwidth-bound regime: every generated token streams all of the model’s weights from memory for about two operations per parameter, so the machine that keeps ResNet-50 busy spends most of a decode step waiting for bytes. MobileNetV2, whose depthwise layers trade arithmetic for a small parameter footprint, and keyword spotting (KWS), the power-bound lighthouse, return where the chapter reaches phone-class and embedded chips. DLRM appears where its embedding lookups, the capacity-bound regime, break the regular access patterns that accelerators assume. The reference machine is the NVIDIA H100, the data-center accelerator this book uses for training and serving examples; its numbers are one generation’s instance of limits that every generation obeys.

Definition 11.1: Hardware acceleration

Hardware acceleration is the practice of mapping work from general-purpose execution onto specialized processors or functional units optimized for a narrower operation class. For ML workloads, that specialization commonly trades some programmability for the compute density \((\PeakRate)\) and performance-per-watt gains that regular tensor operations can exploit.

  1. Significance: An H100 GPU delivers 989 TFLOP/s for dense FP16/BF16 matrix multiplication; against this chapter’s illustrative 1–2 TFLOP/s reference-CPU baseline, this is a 490–990× gap. Its 80 billion transistors devote far more silicon to parallel arithmetic than to branch prediction, out-of-order scheduling, and large caches (Choquette 2023).
  2. Distinction: A general-purpose CPU is designed for flexible execution, low-latency control, and varied workloads. An accelerator instead concentrates resources on a narrower operation class, so it achieves its gains only when the workload exposes the supported operations and enough parallel work to keep its arithmetic units busy.
  3. Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that an accelerator’s advertised peak throughput is the throughput a workload receives. Delivered performance is bounded above by the lower of the compute ceiling and what memory bandwidth can feed (the roofline constraint, developed later in this chapter). A low-arithmetic-intensity kernel can therefore sit at a small fraction of peak FLOP/s no matter how fast the silicon is rated, because it starves for data rather than for arithmetic.

The anatomy of an accelerator is the arrangement of parts that every machine learning accelerator shares: arithmetic units built for tensor operations, on-chip memory that holds operands next to those units, a wide path to off-chip memory, and a host interface through which work arrives. Every inference and every training step on such a machine is a stream of operand movements that ends in multiply-accumulate operations, and the anatomy decides how far each operand travels before it is used. A matrix unit that can retire thousands of multiply-accumulates per cycle sits idle whenever its next operands are still in flight, and an off-chip access can take many processor cycles and cost orders of magnitude more energy than the low-precision operation it feeds. The arithmetic units are the easy part of the design; the rest of the anatomy exists to keep them fed.

The definition becomes concrete in the generic chip of figure 1, which serves as this chapter’s map. External high-bandwidth memory (HBM) feeds shared on-chip storage (an L2 cache), which distributes operands into rows of processing elements, each equipped with a private scratchpad or cache, a matrix unit, a vector unit, and a special function unit. A host interface connects the chip to the CPU that issues its work.

Within each processing element, specialized units partition execution across distinct mathematical primitives: dedicated matrix units (Tensor Cores) execute dense matrix multiplication, vector units evaluate element-wise arithmetic, and special function units (SFUs) approximate transcendental operations such as activations and exponentials. Their number, grouping, and names vary by vendor; some designs arrange them into an explicit 2D systolic grid, and others distribute matrix engines among wide parallel cores.

The memory hierarchy amortizes the cost of data transport across tiers. High-bandwidth memory provides off-chip capacity and throughput, while shared on-chip storage and per-element caches or scratchpads cut off-chip traffic. Because moving a tensor tile across the package boundary costs orders of magnitude more energy than keeping it on chip, compilers and kernels must coordinate tile capacity, reuse, and prefetching to keep operands staged locally. More HBM bandwidth raises the off-chip ceiling, but without local reuse the execution units still stall. The system assumptions appendix (System Assumptions) collects reference specifications for the accelerators this book uses, including the H100.

The host interface links the accelerator to the host CPU, which coordinates execution graphs, asynchronous I/O, and fallback operations while the accelerator executes dispatched kernels. Direct-memory-access engines can overlap host-device transfers with execution, but an operator unsupported by the accelerator backend may require a CPU round-trip. An operator outside the matrix-unit instruction set may instead use vector or other device kernels. These execution boundaries help set the effective speedup envelope. Kernel execution time matters little if transfers, launches, and synchronization dominate end-to-end latency. The three parts of the figure (the processing elements, the memory tiers, and the host link) are the parts this chapter takes apart in turn.

The anatomy embodies the chapter’s central engineering trade-off. General-purpose processors allocate silicon area to complex control logic, speculative execution, branch prediction, and multi-level cache hierarchies to handle arbitrary control flow. An accelerator redirects that transistor budget toward dense arithmetic arrays, dedicated register files, and high-bandwidth memory paths tailored to a narrower workload class. When the software path exposes sufficient tensor parallelism, this specialization yields order-of-magnitude improvements in energy efficiency and throughput per watt. Silicon built for a narrow class of dense tensor operations pays off only because, as the bitter lesson predicts, the general methods that win by exploiting computation keep reducing to those same operations at ever larger scale. The dependence also runs the other way, because scale keeps winning only while accelerators keep lowering the time and energy of each additional operation, so the hardware this chapter studies is part of what sustains the bitter lesson itself.

↩︎ The bitter lesson, the observation that general methods exploiting computation win as computation grows, is established in The Bitter Lesson.

Hardware alone cannot achieve these gains. Algorithms must structure operations to expose data reuse and regular memory access, while silicon architectures must allocate physical units to the mathematical primitives and numeric precisions that algorithms actually execute. That mutual dependence motivates a complementary principle: hardware-software co-design.

Definition 11.2: Hardware-software co-design

Hardware-Software Co-design is an ML accelerator development method that crosses conventional abstraction boundaries, allowing algorithm constraints to inform silicon design and hardware capabilities to shape algorithm formulation.

  1. Significance: On a supported tensor-core path, 8-bit integer (INT8) quantization can deliver multi-fold throughput gains because hardware executes lower-precision operations more densely and moves fewer bytes than an FP32 path; the exact gain depends on the architecture and workload (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a; Dally et al. 2021; Dally 2023).
  2. Distinction: Unlike layered abstraction (where software calls a hardware API without knowing the silicon details), co-design exposes hardware constraints directly to algorithm and compiler authors: data alignment requirements, precision formats, and memory access patterns all become visible inputs to global cross-layer optimization.
  3. Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that co-design is a one-time hardware design choice. In practice, the supported features continue to evolve: NVIDIA Tensor Cores began with FP16 matrix multiplication, later generations added TF32 and broader integer support, and Ampere added acceleration for 2:4 structured sparsity (NVIDIA 2017; NVIDIA Corporation 2020a).

Co-design explains why model compression techniques deliver real speedups. Quantization shows why converting FP32 to INT8 accelerates execution on supported hardware: reduced precision cuts memory traffic, while specialized arithmetic units execute more low-precision operations per cycle than FP32 equivalents (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). Structured pruning improves performance when it produces smaller dense shapes or a sparsity pattern recognized by silicon, whereas arbitrary unstructured sparsity incurs metadata handling and non-coalesced memory accesses that often erase theoretical gains. Evaluating accelerator performance requires tracing this path from workload to silicon: compute primitives, memory hierarchies, roofline diagnosis, mapping and dataflow, and compiler scheduling. The recurring question is why algorithmic improvements frequently fail to deliver proportional end-to-end speedups. Amdahl’s law (principle 8) already answered it for model-side optimizations, since whatever an optimization leaves untouched caps the overall gain. The same bound governs hardware. The theorem below applies the principle to an accelerator, and the only new quantity is the gain, which becomes the accelerator’s path gain \(\AcceleratorGain\).

↩︎ Quantization and its effect on weight payload, memory traffic, and compute cost are established in Numerical Precision: Changing How Values Are Stored.

Theorem 11.1: The fundamental limit of acceleration (Amdahl's law)
Hardware acceleration does not speed up the entire system; it speeds only the baseline-time fraction using the accelerated path. For that fraction \(\ParallelFraction\) and path gain \(\AcceleratorGain\), Amdahl’s law (Amdahl 1967) gives the bound in equation 1. \[ \text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1 - \ParallelFraction) + \frac{\ParallelFraction}{\AcceleratorGain}} \tag{1}\]

  • Accelerated fraction (\(\ParallelFraction\)): Share of baseline time receiving the stated gain, often in matrix multiplication or another supported kernel.
  • Accelerator gain (\(\AcceleratorGain\)): The raw speed advantage of the GPU or Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) over the CPU for the accelerated portion of the workload.
  • Unaccelerated fraction (\(1-\ParallelFraction\)): Work outside the chosen path, such as data loading, host overhead, unsupported operators, and kernel launch latency.

Pitfall: Unaccelerated work caps total speedup. If 10 percent of baseline time is unaffected (\(\ParallelFraction=0.9\)), even infinite path gain (\(\AcceleratorGain=\infty\)) yields at most 10\(\times\) overall. Once the accelerated component is fast enough, unaffected work dominates.

Amdahl, Gene M. 1967. “Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities.” Proceedings of the April 18-20, 1967, Spring Joint Computer Conference on - AFIPS ’67 (Spring), AFIPS ’67 (spring), 483–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560.

1 Amdahl’s law: Maps onto the iron law only after the proposed change is specified. If a faster tensor unit reduces the computation term \((\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\) but leaves data transfer and fixed latency unchanged, those unaffected terms bound total speedup. A different accelerator or memory system may improve bandwidth as well. The unaccelerated fraction is therefore defined by the intervention, not by a permanent classification of each term as serial.

Hardware acceleration targets specific terms in the iron law of ML systems, which decomposes end-to-end time into data movement \((\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)\), computation \((\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw))\), and fixed latency \((\Latency)\). Data selection reduced the number of samples processed (\(\text{Samples/Task}\), shrinking both \(\Operations\) and input traffic \(\DataVolume\)), and model compression reduced the operations and bytes per sample (\(\text{FLOPs/Sample}\) and weight traffic \(\DataVolume\)). Hardware acceleration instead reduces the realized time per operation (\(\text{Seconds/FLOP}\)) by improving \(\PeakRate\), \(\EfficiencyHw\), and \(\Bandwidth\). Which of these physical terms an upgrade actually improves determines its accelerated fraction under Amdahl’s law.1

↩︎ The decomposition of execution time into data, compute, and latency terms is established in Iron Law of ML Systems.

This dynamic explains why hardware upgrades frequently fail to produce proportional end-to-end speedups. Figure 2 maps system speedup across accelerator gain (\(\AcceleratorGain\)) and accelerated fraction (\(\ParallelFraction\)), charting where those returns diminish. Where the unaccelerated fraction \(1-\ParallelFraction\) remains substantial, the white contour curves flatten horizontally into the unaccelerated-bound regime, bounding total speedup at the \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) asymptote regardless of how far \(\AcceleratorGain\) scales along the horizontal axis. Because \(\ParallelFraction\) differs substantially across workload archetypes running on identical hardware, a workload’s vertical position on this map determines whether an accelerator investment pays off or stalls on non-matrix operations.

Checkpoint 11.1: The parallelism gate

These checks turn Amdahl’s bound into a hardware-selection test.

Amdahl’s reality

The serial bottleneck becomes concrete on real hardware, where the same accelerator that nears its parallel ceiling on one workload can stall on another. The comparison below uses the INT8 (8-bit integer) path, whose advantage over FP32 or FP16 has two sources. Each operand occupies a half or a quarter of the bytes, and an 8-bit multiplier occupies far less silicon area than a floating-point one, so the same die holds more multiply-accumulate (MAC) units. Two workloads on an NVIDIA H100 with different unaccelerated fractions show how that fraction governs whether this peak INT8 advantage becomes realized speedup. A second look at the decode case then separates that limit from a different one, bandwidth-boundedness.

↪ Order-of-magnitude throughput, bandwidth, and capacity for each accelerator class are collected for reference in Accelerator classes.

Lighthouse 11.1: An illustrative Amdahl budget on H100
Illustrative ResNet-50 inference on NVIDIA H100:

  • Assume H100 provides \(\AcceleratorGain\) = 247× on matrix multiplication relative to a server CPU without matrix extensions (1979 TOPS INT8 vs. ~8 TOPS) (Choquette 2023). The CPU’s INT8 rate is a scenario assumption for this budget, not the FP32 peak of the reference CPU used elsewhere in the chapter.
  • Assume \(\ParallelFraction\) = 0.95: 95 percent of baseline time receives that gain, while 5 percent remains in data loading, preprocessing, postprocessing, and other work. \[ \text{$\text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1-0.95) + \frac{0.95}{247}} = \frac{1}{0.05 + 0.0038} \approx 18.6\times$} \] The 247× path gain produces only 18.6× end-to-end speedup because the 5 percent unaffected fraction sets the ceiling.

Contrast with GPT-2 (autoregressive):

  • For GPT-2 token generation, assume \(\ParallelFraction\) = 0.80; the remaining 20 percent includes host overhead, sampling, and decoding work outside the accelerated matrix path. \[ \text{$\text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1-0.80) + \frac{0.80}{247}} = \frac{1}{0.20 + 0.0032} \approx 4.9\times$} \] Less token-generation time receives the assumed gain, so even an infinite path gain yields at most \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) = 5×.

This calculation still overstates the decode path gain. Decode is bandwidth bound, so its accelerated path runs at the rate weights stream from memory rather than at the INT8 TOPS rate. The relevant ratio is the H100’s memory bandwidth over the reference CPU socket’s, 67× (a different path from the host-DRAM link used below). INT8 helps decode on either machine by halving the bytes each weight occupies relative to FP16, not by multiplying faster. With that gain the bound falls from 4.9× to 4.7×, barely moving, because the unaccelerated fraction already dominates. Two distinct limits are at work. Bandwidth-boundedness shrinks \(\AcceleratorGain\), whereas the unaccelerated fraction caps what any \(\AcceleratorGain\) can deliver. Serving optimizations attack both. Batching raises the work done per weight byte fetched. Speculative decoding, developed in Model Serving, lets a small draft model propose several tokens that the full model then verifies in one step, reducing the number of sequential full-model steps.

Whether an operation is limited by compute rate or by data movement dictates both hardware selection and software optimization. Under the arithmetic intensity law (principle 6), upgrading to an accelerator with \(10\times\) higher peak compute yields negligible speedup if data delivery is the binding bottleneck. The roofline model, previewed in Matching workloads to hardware, makes this diagnosis (Williams et al. 2009). It compares an operation’s arithmetic intensity, the ratio of operations to bytes of memory traffic (FLOP/byte), with the hardware’s ridge point. An operation below the ridge is bandwidth bound, the regime the roofline literature calls memory bound; an operation above it is compute bound. GPT-2 decode and ResNet-50 sit on opposite sides of that line, a difference the Amdahl budget above already registered in the decode path gain. Section 11.6 turns the classification into numbers once the compute units and memory systems that set the two ceilings have been examined.

↩︎ The arithmetic-intensity spectrum that separates the workload signatures of the major architectures is established in Arithmetic intensity across workloads.

The chapter builds the machine from the bottom up (table 1). Compute primitives and compute units supply the arithmetic side of the anatomy, ending with the INT8 and sparse paths that ResNet-50’s profile depends on, and memory systems supply the other side, from registers to host memory. Performance bounds then combine the two into the roofline’s ceilings and show which ResNet-50 layers clear the H100’s ridge at FP16 and which fall below it at INT8; this is the chapter’s midpoint, marked by a checkpoint. The second half asks how software reaches those ceilings, through hardware mapping and then the compilers and runtimes that make its choices automatically. Three shorter sections widen the view to work beyond one accelerator, heterogeneous systems-on-chip, and the choice of an accelerator for a workload and a budget.

The first stage of the accelerator’s anatomy begins with a simpler question: why build specialized silicon for tensor math at all, rather than running those operations on general-purpose processors?

Self-Check: Question

  1. An ML engineer upgrades a training cluster from baseline CPUs to NVIDIA H100 GPUs, providing an accelerator compute gain of \(G_{\text{accel}} = 250\times\) on matrix operations. If data preprocessing, serialization, and CPU-GPU transfers constitute \(10\%\) of the baseline execution time (\(p = 0.90\)), what is the maximum achievable end-to-end speedup according to Amdahl’s Law?

    1. Approximately \(9.6\times\) (bounded by the theoretical ceiling of \(10\times\))
    2. Approximately \(25\times\) (bounded by the memory bandwidth ratio)
    3. Approximately \(125\times\) (half of the matrix unit throughput multiplier)
    4. Approximately \(250\times\) (scaling linearly with the raw compute gain)

  2. Explain why a compute-only accelerator upgrade can help high-reuse convolutional training more than batch-1 autoregressive decoding, even when the new device advertises much higher peak arithmetic throughput \(R_{\text{peak}}\).

  3. True or False: In the iron law of ML systems decomposition (\(\text{Time} = \frac{D_{\text{vol}}}{\text{BW}} + \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}}} + L_{\text{lat}}\)), the unaccelerated fraction \((1-p)\) is an immutable, fixed property of the model architecture regardless of the hardware intervention.

  4. The metric defined as the ratio of floating-point operations performed to bytes of memory traffic transferred across a specific memory hierarchy interface is called ____.

Which term is most directly improved when replacing standard FP32 GEMM instructions with a supported mixed-precision Tensor Core path for the same operation?

    2. Only the fixed invocation latency \(L_{\text{lat}}\) of the kernel driver

11.2 Hardware Specialization

General-purpose processors dedicate substantial silicon area and power to instruction fetch, branch prediction, out-of-order scheduling, and cache coherence, machinery built for arbitrary control flow that yields poor arithmetic density on regular, dense linear algebra. When Google deployed its first Tensor Processing Unit (TPU v1) into production data centers alongside contemporary CPUs and NVIDIA K80 GPUs, stripping away that general-purpose control machinery in favor of a dedicated matrix array produced an immediate efficiency jump (example 11.1). Whenever an algorithmic pattern becomes sufficiently dominant and structured, specialized hardware outperforms general-purpose platforms by replacing dynamic control hardware with dense arithmetic arrays and software-managed data movement.

Example 11.1: The TPU v1 vs. K80 efficiency gap
Scenario: In 2015, Google deployed its first Tensor Processing Unit (TPU v1) into production data centers, comparing its throughput and energy efficiency against general-purpose NVIDIA K80 GPUs (Jouppi et al. 2017).

Diagnosis: The K80 was a programmable GPU designed to support a broader mix of graphics and compute workloads. The TPU v1 domain-specific architecture (DSA) made a narrower, inference-focused design choice, pairing a large 8-bit systolic matrix unit with software-managed memory and simpler control.

Systems lesson: On the six Google inference workloads and contemporary CPU/GPU baselines evaluated in the TPU paper, tailoring silicon to the dominant matrix operations delivered 15–30\(\times\) higher throughput and 30–80\(\times\) better performance per watt (Jouppi et al. 2017). Those ratios describe the evaluated systems, not every workload.

2 TPU (tensor processing unit): The first TPU made a deliberately narrow design choice, centering the design on a single \(256{\times}256\) systolic array for 8-bit matrix multiplication and avoiding much of the control machinery required by a general-purpose core (Jouppi et al. 2017). That trade buys high compute density on dense matrix multiplication at the cost of flexibility. Irregular or branch-heavy code remains a poor fit, and compiler tiling, padding, and layer dimensions determine how fully the array is used.

Chen, Tianshi, Zidong Du, Ninghui Sun, Jia Wang, Chengyong Wu, Yunji Chen, and Olivier Temam. 2014. “DianNao: A Small-Footprint High-Throughput Accelerator for Ubiquitous Machine-Learning.” Proceedings of the 19th International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS ’14), 269–84. https://doi.org/10.1145/2541940.2541967.

In D·A·M terms, this efficiency gain stems from tailoring machine resources to algorithmic structure. The TPU2 replaced hardware caches with software-managed buffers and routed data directly between neighboring arithmetic units, raising data reuse and cutting off-chip traffic. The cost is rigidity. Irregular memory access, dynamic control flow, or an unsupported numeric precision stalls a fixed-function data path and leaves expensive silicon idle. Every modern ML accelerator, from DianNao-class designs (Chen et al. 2014) to GPUs with Tensor Cores, strikes its own balance between specialization and flexibility, following a pattern that began decades before deep learning.

11.2.1 Specialized computing

On a late-1970s microprocessor without floating-point hardware, a single 32-bit floating-point multiply required a software routine of dozens of integer shift-and-add instructions, turning scientific and signal-processing loops into an instruction-fetch bottleneck. Hardware specialization emerges whenever one computational pattern becomes a bottleneck that general-purpose processors cannot scale past. The Intel 8087 coprocessor (1980) executed floating-point operations directly in hardware (Palmer 1980), and the Intel 486DX (1989) later moved the floating-point unit onto the CPU die itself (Hennessy and Patterson 2017). That cycle—specializing silicon to relieve an acute bottleneck and integrating it once the capability proves universal—recurs in every later era, and so does its limit. Dedicated silicon removes the instruction overhead around a dominant operation, but the overall gain is bounded by how much of the run time that operation occupies.

Lyons, Richard G. 2011. Understanding Digital Signal Processing. 3rd ed. Prentice Hall.

Graphics supplied the second lesson, throughput over latency. A CPU spends most of its silicon on control logic, branch prediction, and caches that minimize the latency of a single instruction stream, which buys nothing when identical arithmetic must be applied to millions of independent pixels. GPUs reallocated that silicon to dense arrays of arithmetic units, and when unified shader architectures (2006) replaced separate vertex and pixel pipelines with arrays of identical programmable cores, the GPU became a general-purpose parallel processor (Owens et al. 2008). Digital signal processors such as Texas Instruments’ TMS32010 (1983) contributed the memory organization. To meet hard real-time deadlines, they replaced caches, whose misses introduce variable latency, with software-managed scratchpads feeding dedicated MAC data paths (Lyons 2011). ML accelerators inherit both lessons.

The payoff arrived in 2012, when AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al. 2012) won the ImageNet competition after training on two consumer GPUs, the co-design result examined in The deep learning era and the infrastructure bottleneck. Its dense 2D convolutions mapped directly onto thousands of GPU arithmetic lanes. In D·A·M terms, the machine constraint had dictated which algorithms were feasible, and aligning the algorithm’s parallel structure with throughput-oriented hardware lifted it.

Across five eras from the 1980s to the 2020s (figure 3), specialization moved from discrete coprocessors such as the Intel 8087 FPU and TMS32010 DSP through graphics engines and dedicated media codecs to deep-learning tensor arrays and wafer-scale hardware. Each era’s specialized unit targets a different bottleneck, yet the principles modern accelerators depend on (dedicating silicon to the dominant operation, staging operands in local memory, and minimizing off-chip data movement) were all in place before deep learning arrived.

11.2.2 Domain-specific architectures

A general-purpose CPU core spends most of its energy on instruction fetch and decode, branch prediction, speculative execution, and cache coherence rather than arithmetic: executing one scalar instruction can burn hundreds of picojoules of control overhead just to perform a floating-point operation that costs a few picojoules. For decades, Moore’s law3 (Moore 1998) and Dennard scaling (Dennard et al. 1974) hid that overhead by letting operating voltage fall as transistors shrank, so clock frequencies rose at constant power density. When leakage current halted voltage scaling in the mid-2000s, frequencies stalled against the power wall of Physical Constraints on Deployment. Adding more general-purpose cores then ran into Amdahl’s law and dark silicon, the thermal limit under which only a fraction of a chip’s transistors can switch at full speed simultaneously (Esmaeilzadeh et al. 2011). As Hennessy and Patterson (2019) argued in their Turing Lecture, the way past this wall is domain-specific architectures (DSAs),4 hardware that gives up general-purpose control machinery to spend its power budget directly on the operations a target domain performs.

3 Moore’s law: Gordon Moore’s 1965 observation, revised in 1975, that the number of transistors per chip doubles roughly every two years (Moore 1998). It describes density, not performance; performance tracked density only while Dennard scaling held.

Moore, G. E. 1998. “Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits.” Proceedings of the IEEE 86 (1): 82–85. https://doi.org/10.1109/jproc.1998.658762.
Dennard, Robert H., Frank H. Gaensslen, Hwa-Nien Yu, Victor L. Rideout, Elias Bassous, and Antoine R. LeBlanc. 1974. “Design of Ion-Implanted MOSFET’s with Very Small Physical Dimensions.” IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits 9 (5): 256–68. https://doi.org/10.1109/jssc.1974.1050511.
Esmaeilzadeh, Hadi, Emily Blem, Renee St. Amant, Karthikeyan Sankaralingam, and Doug Burger. 2011. “Dark Silicon and the End of Multicore Scaling.” Proceedings of the 38th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 365–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/2000064.2000108.

4 DSA (domain-specific architecture): A DSA that excels at dense matrix multiplication may perform worse than a CPU on irregular workloads such as graph traversal, so its gain on the target domain must justify the software, compiler, and ecosystem cost of a narrower machine (Hennessy and Patterson 2019, 2017).

Hennessy, John L., and David A. Patterson. 2019. “A New Golden Age for Computer Architecture.” Communications of the ACM 62 (2): 48–60. https://doi.org/10.1145/3282307.
Hennessy, John L., and David A. Patterson. 2017. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. 6th ed. Morgan Kaufmann.
Sullivan, Gary J., Jens-Rainer Ohm, Woo-Jin Han, and Thomas Wiegand. 2012. “Overview of the High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) Standard.” IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology 22 (12): 1649–68. https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2012.2221191.
Turakhia, Yatish, Gill Bejerano, and William J. Dally. 2018. “Darwin: A Genomics Co-Processor Provides up to 15,000X Acceleration on Long Read Assembly.” Proceedings of the Twenty-Third International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS), 199–213. https://doi.org/10.1145/3173162.3173193.
Bedford Taylor, Michael. 2017. “The Evolution of Bitcoin Hardware.” Computer 50 (9): 58–66. https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.2017.3571056.

A DSA wins by specializing every layer of the machine around the workload’s invariants. Its data path is custom-built. Matrix units in AI accelerators are often systolic arrays, grid-like networks of processing elements that compute and forward data directly to neighboring units. A value fetched once from on-chip memory is therefore reused across an entire row or column of multiply-accumulate operations instead of returning to a register file after each use. Its memory hierarchy follows the workload’s reuse pattern, with software-managed scratchpads and prefetching replacing hardware-managed caches for deterministic tensor streams. Its instruction set encodes coarse tensor operations, so one macro-instruction configures thousands of arithmetic units. The same recipe produced smartphone video codecs, genomics aligners, and cryptographic application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) wherever a kernel stabilized (Sullivan et al. 2012; Turakhia et al. 2018; Bedford Taylor 2017).

The pressure to specialize has grown because model demand has outrun single-device hardware scaling. The measured trend is the historical training-compute curve charted in Introduction, whose fitted doubling time runs from 3.4 to about 6 months depending on the window, far faster than the roughly two-year doubling of transistor density (Amodei and Hernandez 2018; Epoch AI 2024). No single chip closes a gap that compounds at that rate; parallelism and co-design must close the rest.

Amodei, Dario, and Danny Hernandez. 2018. “AI and Compute.” OpenAI Blog 2.
Epoch AI. 2024. Machine Learning Trends. Epoch AI Research Database.

↩︎ The measured growth of training compute and its doubling time are established in Three Dimensions of ML Efficiency.

11.2.3 Machine learning hardware specialization

That compounding gap between model demand and transistor scaling turned into an operational crisis at Google in 2013, when an internal projection showed that three minutes of daily voice search per user would require doubling the company’s global CPU fleet just to serve neural-network inference (example 11.2), the projection that launched the TPU v1 program introduced at the start of this section. Many important neural-network workloads concentrate their arithmetic in regular tensor operations, such as dense matrix multiplications and convolutions, with substantial data parallelism, predictable reuse, and tolerance for reduced precision. Other ML operations remain irregular, bandwidth bound, or too small to fill a wide engine, so an accelerator need not speed up every part of a model. Hardware built to exploit the regular portion forms the class of ML accelerators.

Example 11.2: The TPU capacity cliff
Scenario: Google projected in 2013 that user adoption of voice-search speech recognition (3 minutes/day/user) would require doubling global data center capacity to run CPU-based neural network inference (Jouppi et al. 2017).

Diagnosis: General-purpose CPU server capacity was economically unable to absorb the exponential growth in inference FLOPs, threatening a capital infrastructure bottleneck.

Systems lesson: Custom hardware acceleration becomes a candidate when workload volume makes the existing fleet uneconomical. Workload reuse, supported operations, development cost, and server total cost of ownership determine whether a custom ASIC is preferable to software changes or other hardware.

The fleet projection exposed how little of a CPU’s rated throughput survives on dense tensor layers. Take the chapter’s reference CPU, the low end of the 1–2 TFLOP/s baseline used in the definition of hardware acceleration, and assume it sustains 5 percent–10 percent of its peak on a neural network workload. The upper endpoint then delivers approximately 100 GFLOP/s (billions of floating-point operations per second). CPUs optimize for single-thread performance and irregular memory access, whereas neural networks require extensive parallelism and predictable data streams, and a single layer that touches gigabytes of parameters overwhelms cache hierarchies designed for smaller working sets.

The deeper mismatch is energy. Per event, accessing a 32-bit value from DRAM costs about 640 pJ in the 45 nm estimates of Horowitz (2014), roughly 173× the 3.7 pJ of one FP32 multiply, the same ratio Energy Cost of Moving vs. Computing on a 32-Bit Value reported for the data pipeline. The roughly 145-fold gap quoted with the iron law in Iron Law of ML Systems comes from the same table but compared one DRAM byte, a quarter of this 32-bit access, with one FP16 operation. Exact values vary by technology node and design, but a gap of two orders of magnitude, the energy-movement principle (7), makes data movement a primary optimization target (Sze et al. 2017). Purpose-built accelerators such as TPUs sustain high utilization on dense kernels because systolic arrays and similar structures maximize data reuse while minimizing movement.

5 Von Neumann bottleneck: Separating storage from compute requires instructions and data to cross interfaces rather than remain in local registers. The exact cost of each crossing changes with technology and operation, but locality remains a first-order design concern.

Data access can dominate the energy budget of a memory-intensive kernel.5 On a logarithmic scale, representative 45 nm operation energies span more than four orders of magnitude, from an INT8 addition (\(0.03\text{ pJ}\)) and an FP32 multiply (\(3.7\text{ pJ}\)) to an off-chip DRAM fetch (\(640\text{ pJ}\)) (figure 4). This ladder is the chapter’s single reference for what moving a value costs; later sections cite it rather than restate it.

Training and inference load an accelerator differently. Training computes gradients, typically in mixed precision with lower-precision tensor operations and higher-precision accumulation (Micikevicius et al. 2018), and backpropagation retains or recomputes activations, raising memory demand. Inference requires only the forward path and may use INT8 or INT4 when the model and kernels support it. The service objective, whether tail latency, throughput, cost, or energy, then decides which accelerator fits.

↩︎ The activation memory that backpropagation must retain is established in Activation memory requirements.

Definition 11.3: ML accelerator

Machine Learning Accelerators are processors or specialized units designed primarily for common neural-network tensor operations and dataflows. They pursue high \(\PeakRate\) and data reuse on matching workloads by devoting more resources to arithmetic and local data movement than a general-purpose execution path can.

  1. Significance: An ML accelerator’s defining feature is not raw arithmetic alone but a balanced path that supplies operands and retains reusable values nearby. The H100 provides 3.35 TB/s of device-memory bandwidth, about 16.8× the illustrative 200 GB/s host-DRAM path used here (Choquette 2023). This is a ceiling comparison, not a guarantee: sufficient arithmetic intensity, concurrency, and reuse are still required to approach its 989 TFLOP/s dense FP16/BF16 peak.
  2. Distinction: The gains are conditional on operation support, parallel work, regular data access, and a software stack that selects the intended path. An ML accelerator can be orders of magnitude faster than a reference CPU on large dense matrix multiplication, yet lose much of that advantage on small, irregular, synchronization-heavy, or control-heavy workloads. Transfers and unsupported operators can dominate even when the accelerated kernel itself is fast.
  3. Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that ML accelerators always accelerate ML. Approaching peak throughput requires a compatible precision, operation shape, layout, and enough parallel work to keep the relevant units busy, and memory and interconnect paths must sustain that work. A batch-1 autoregressive request may therefore use only a small fraction of a large training accelerator’s arithmetic capacity even though the same device performs well on batched prefill or training.

Deployment context decides which constraint binds. In data centers it is often time-to-result for training large models. An NVIDIA H100 trades hundreds of watts of power for high throughput (Choquette 2023), and Google’s TPU v4 makes a similar trade through systolic arrays and high-bandwidth memory (Jouppi et al. 2023); whether either lowers total cost depends on utilization, rental price, workload scaling, and the electricity rate.

At the edge, the priority shifts toward energy per inference and hard latency or power limits. A smartphone camera or always-on audio path inside a few-watt budget cannot adopt a data center memory system, so edge architectures reduce movement through local scratchpads, tight integration, and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. Because the binding constraint differs by setting, no single architecture dominates, yet the memory wall governs both. Data center chips buy capacity and bandwidth with HBM, while edge chips depend on proximity and reuse.

11.2.4 The integration bottleneck

Packing thousands of multiply-accumulate units onto a die buys nothing if those units spend most cycles stalled waiting for operands to cross the memory hierarchy. Once specialized arrays make arithmetic cheap and abundant (Palmer 1980; Sze et al. 2017; Jouppi et al. 2017), the dominant hardware difficulty shifts from computing products to feeding the units that compute them. This integration bottleneck is the memory wall seen from inside the accelerator: transporting operands and results through the memory hierarchy quickly and efficiently enough to keep thousands of parallel compute units busy. Specialized silicon delivers its performance-per-watt advantage only when the workload’s demand concentrates into regular operations that align with the hardware’s data paths.

6 Scratchpad memory: When a compiler can determine a tensor kernel’s access pattern, it can explicitly stage tiles in fast, software-controlled local memory. This avoids some tag, replacement, and coherence machinery, but transfers, synchronization, banking, and capacity must be scheduled correctly. Scratchpads complement rather than universally replace caches because irregular or shared data may still benefit from hardware management. Google’s TPU v1, for example, used a 24 MB software-managed Unified Buffer for intermediate activations, while weights and instructions used other paths (Jouppi et al. 2017).

Jouppi, Norman P., Cliff Young, Nishant Patil, David Patterson, Gaurav Agrawal, Raminder Bajwa, Sarah Bates, et al. 2017. “In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit.” Proceedings of the 44th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, ISCA ’17, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1145/3079856.3080246.

Neural-network kernels make this integration bottleneck tractable because their arithmetic, dataflow, and numerical requirements reinforce one another. Large matrix multiplications and convolutions expose abundant data parallelism that dense processing-element arrays can execute concurrently. Because static or compiled tensor graphs move those operands along predictable paths, compilers can tile and stage transfers into local scratchpads6 instead of relying exclusively on hardware-managed caches. Those staged operands also tolerate reduced precision, allowing supported 8-bit or 4-bit paths to pack more values into each scratchpad and multiply them more densely (Dally et al. 2021; Dally 2023). Workloads dominated by dynamic control flow, large embedding tables, small tensors, variable shapes, or strict precision requirements break these assumptions and remain bound by memory latency and irregular access.

Because off-chip DRAM transfers carry that 173× energy penalty over an FP32 multiply, accelerator architects allocate silicon area and thermal budgets to stacked HBM, wide on-chip SRAM, and software-managed scratchpads rather than packing in additional floating-point logic.7 Those are the memory tiers drawn in figure 1, and they occupy as much of the design as the arithmetic units they feed.

7 HBM: The A100 and H100 generations provide 2.0–3.4 TB/s of device-memory bandwidth through stacked memory and wide interfaces, compared with 760 GB/s for the GDDR6X reference used here (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a; Choquette 2023). Raising the bandwidth ceiling can move some kernels toward the compute-bound side of the roofline, but only if their access pattern and arithmetic intensity can use it. HBM also increases packaging and system cost, so its value depends on the workload’s bandwidth demand.

The specialization evident in processing elements, vector pipelines, and tiered scratchpads reflects the computational profile of neural networks, which repeatedly invoke a compact set of linear-algebraic and element-wise primitives. Within the D·A·M framework, an algorithmic change produces a wall-clock speedup only when its computational structure and memory access pattern map onto these primitives; one that cuts theoretical operations without aligning with the hardware’s data paths leaves compute units starved. The next section identifies those primitives, beginning with the multiply-accumulate that carries nearly all of ResNet-50’s arithmetic.

  1. What primary physical limitation brought about the end of Dennard scaling in the mid-2000s, necessitating the transition from increasing CPU clock frequencies to domain-specific hardware accelerators?

    1. Lithography light diffraction preventing further reduction of transistor gate length below \(1\,\mu\text{m}\)
    2. Inability to lower operating voltage proportionally with transistor size, leading to unsustainable power density and heat dissipation limits
    3. Quantum tunneling in copper interconnect lines preventing data transmission between arithmetic units
    4. Depletion of global silicon substrate supplies requiring migration to gallium nitride semiconductors

  2. Contrast the architectural trade-offs of software-managed scratchpad memory (such as Google TPUv1’s Unified Buffer) with hardware-managed cache hierarchies when executing large-scale tensor workloads.

  3. Place the following computing milestones in chronological order (from earliest to most recent) as hardware evolved toward modern AI accelerators:

  1. Introduction of dedicated Tensor Cores and TPUs for deep learning matrix operations
  2. Emergence of fixed-function media codecs and network processors for video/packet streaming
  3. Integration of floating-point units (FPUs) and digital signal processors (DSPs) as discrete coprocessors
  4. General-purpose programmable GPUs and SIMD instruction set extensions for 3D graphics and multimedia

11.3 Compute Primitives

A single forward pass through a neural network layer can issue millions or billions of MAC operations, and executing them one scalar instruction at a time would swamp the processor in instruction-fetch and register-access overhead. Across fully connected, convolutional, and attention layers, learned linear transformations reduce to these repeated MACs, whose regular tensor structure exposes the parallel work and operand reuse that hardware specialization requires. MACs do not dominate every model or phase (normalization, routing, indexing, communication, and element-wise operations can become limiting), but they account for much of the peak arithmetic capacity in modern ML accelerators. Whether they dominate elapsed time still depends on tensor shape, data movement, and the surrounding operators.

The hardware units that exploit these patterns are AI compute primitives: specialized functional blocks, each optimized for a particular class of operation. Three primitives are especially common in accelerators, each targeting a distinct computational pattern found in neural networks; at the framework level, a single declarative statement encapsulates thousands of their arithmetic operations (listing 1).

Beneath this API call, an autograd or compilation engine lowers the layer into a computational graph. Listing 2 exposes a bulk matrix multiplication and bias broadcast, followed by an optional element-wise activation; the activation is a separate stage rather than an implicit part of the shown Dense call.

While graph representations group these steps into coarse tensor operators, execution on physical hardware requires scheduling individual scalar operations. Lowering the matrix multiplication to loop nests (listing 3) makes the execution structure explicit: three nested iterations traverse the batch, output feature, and reduction dimensions, establishing \(\mathcal{O}(\BatchSize\times \LayerInputWidth \times \LayerOutputWidth)\) arithmetic complexity.

These nested loops expose three recurring computational patterns: element-wise operations along vectors, matrix-level multiply-accumulate reductions, and nonlinear transformations. Their ubiquity justifies dedicated hardware execution paths: vector pipelines stream independent elements and reductions, matrix engines organize multiply-accumulate grids across spatial tiles, and special-function units approximate nonlinear math. The boundaries between these units are architectural rather than mathematical; an optimizing compiler frequently fuses operations across all three paths within a single kernel invocation to eliminate intermediate memory traffic.

11.3.1 Vector operations

In the scalar loop nest of listing 3, evaluating a batch of 32 samples through a 256-to-512 dense layer requires 4.2M MACs. A scalar processor must fetch and decode separate instructions to load each input-weight pair, multiply-accumulate them, and advance the loop counters. Vector architectures eliminate this per-element control overhead by packing multiple data elements into wide register files (typically 128 to 512 bits) and applying a single decoded instruction across parallel execution lanes simultaneously.

RISC-V,8 an open instruction-set architecture (ISA) with a standardized vector extension (Waterman et al. 2013), provides a concrete vehicle for this execution model. The contiguous loads in listing 4 assume that the selected weight column has been packed into a contiguous vector; the row-major weights[k, m] access in the scalar example is otherwise strided. In RISC-V vector assembly, code does not depend on a fixed hardware width. The instruction vsetvli queries the hardware to determine how many elements fit into available registers, the code processes that chunk, and the loop repeats until all features are exhausted.

8 RISC-V (reduced instruction set computer V): The open ISA allows hardware teams to add custom ML instructions, including vector dot products, activation functions, and sparse tensor operations, without changing the base ISA. The trade-off is software ecosystem maturity: custom extensions require corresponding compiler, library, and runtime support, which can limit portability and increase integration work.

Waterman, Andrew, Yunsup Lee, Rimas Avizienis, Henry Cook, David Patterson, and Krste Asanovic. 2013. “The RISC-V Instruction Set.” 2013 IEEE Hot Chips 25 Symposium (HCS), 1–1. https://doi.org/10.1109/hotchips.2013.7478332.

Each pass of the loop in listing 4 asks the hardware how many 32-bit elements fit in its vector registers (vsetvli) and loads that many input and weight elements with two wide loads (vle32.v). It then multiplies them lane by lane (vfmul.vv), reduces the products into a partial sum (vfredusum.vs), and advances the pointers until no elements remain. One decoded instruction thus does the work of a whole chunk of scalar instructions.

Across iterations, the vector multiply instruction processes multiple data elements concurrently while wide loads amortize instruction decode and memory-request overhead. Because the runtime vector length dynamically adapts to the implementation’s hardware width (VLEN), the identical binary executes correctly on both narrow embedded vector units and wide data-center pipelines. For this 256-feature workload, an 8-lane implementation breaks the reduction into approximately 524,288 vector chunks across the batch.

Beyond dense inner products, deep learning workloads rely on a broader set of vector instructions. Table 2 maps these primitive vector operations to the specific neural network layers that depend on them.

The benefit extends beyond instruction count. Contiguous vector loads can use memory interfaces efficiently, and control overhead is amortized across several data elements. Gather, scatter, masking, and short tails may use fewer lanes or require extra memory transactions, so vector width alone does not guarantee proportional speedup. The architectural pattern is not new. The Cray-19 used vector registers and pipelined functional units for scientific computing in the 1970s (Jordan 1982); modern ML processors apply related principles at much larger commercial scale. In ResNet-50 the vector path carries the ReLU after every convolution and the residual addition that closes every bottleneck block. Each touches every activation element once and performs about one operation per element, so on its own it is limited by how fast the activations stream past, not by lane count.

9 Cray-1 vector legacy: The Cray-1 (1975) used 64-element vector registers with pipelined functional units, allowing a stream of elements to advance through arithmetic operations without issuing one scalar instruction per element. Modern accelerators extend the same principles of wide registers, pipelined execution, and data reuse to vector and matrix tiles.

Jordan, T. L. 1982. “A Guide to Parallel Computation and Some Cray-1 Experiences.” In Parallel Computations. Elsevier. https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-12-592101-5.50006-3.

Vector operations excel at element-wise transformations such as activation functions, where each output depends only on its corresponding input. Neural networks, however, also require structured computations where each output depends on all inputs, the weighted sums that define layer transformations. These many-to-many operations naturally express themselves as matrix multiplications, the second compute primitive.

11.3.2 Matrix operations

Evaluating a dense layer one vector dot product at a time wastes reuse: each weight row is loaded for one sample and discarded before the next sample in the batch arrives, and each input vector is re-read for every output neuron. Matrix multiplication eliminates this redundant traffic by organizing work across two-dimensional tiles of weights, activations, and gradients, accounting for much of the arithmetic in dense neural networks (Goodfellow et al. 2016). Hardware and libraries tile those dimensions so blocks of weights and activations are reused across an entire tile while partial sums accumulate locally, though small or irregular matrices can still leave tile capacity unused.

Matrix operations in neural networks

Neural network computations decompose into hierarchical matrix operations. Listing 5 captures this hierarchy through a linear layer that transforms input features into output neurons over a batch. Its expanded mathematics uses a column-batch convention and adds an optional ReLU; this illustrates the arithmetic rather than the framework API’s internal tensor layout or an activation implicit in nn.Linear.

The scale of this matrix work follows from the layer dimensions. Each output neuron (512 total) must process all input features (256 total) for every sample in the batch (32 samples). The weight matrix alone contains 256 \(\times\) 512 = 131,072 parameters that define these transformations, illustrating why efficient matrix multiplication dominates performance considerations.

Neural networks employ matrix operations across architectural patterns beyond simple linear layers. Convolution operations transform into matrix multiplications through the im2col technique,10 enabling efficient execution on matrix-optimized hardware. Listing 6 illustrates these applications.

10 Im2col (image-to-column): The im2col lowering of Computational mapping turns convolution into a matrix multiplication by unfolding each receptive-field patch into one row or column of a dense matrix. An explicit materialization can duplicate overlapping values and expand storage by up to roughly the kernel area before edge, stride, and channel effects are considered. Production libraries often use implicit-GEMM or direct-convolution kernels to obtain matrix-friendly execution without materializing the full expanded matrix.

These examples differ in tensor shape and reuse pattern, which determines how efficiently each multiplication occupies a matrix unit. Linear layers reuse one weight matrix across a batch; attention forms projections and then a token-to-token score matrix; convolution reuses each kernel across many image patches. Expressing all three as matrix multiplication exposes a common interface to hardware, but it does not make their execution costs identical. Batch size, sequence length, channel count, and tiling determine whether operands are reused locally or repeatedly fetched from memory. For ResNet-50 the lowering is nearly total: every convolution and the final fully connected layer become matrix multiplications, so almost all of its operations run on whatever matrix hardware the accelerator provides. The INT8 profile of Model Compression is in effect a statement about that hardware.

Matrix operations hardware acceleration

Accelerators therefore need units that handle whole tiles. Listing 7 demonstrates a representative dedicated matrix unit that processes an entire \(16{\times}16\) block at once, illustrating why matrix instructions and Tensor Cores can deliver much higher throughput than scalar or vector-only execution paths (NVIDIA 2017; Intel Corporation 2021a).

The illustrative unit operates on matrix tiles rather than individual elements. A full \(16{\times}16{\times}16\) tile product contains \(16^3=4{,}096\) multiply-accumulate operations, but the cycles required depend on the actual instruction and architecture. Sustained throughput also depends on the number of matrix units, operand precision, issue rate, pipeline behavior, and whether memory can keep the units fed. Matrix units complement vector execution by accelerating structured many-to-many transformations.

Much like vector processing, matrix acceleration has deep historical roots; digital signal processors (DSPs) and graphics processors optimized matrix computations in the 1980s–1990s for image processing, scientific computing, and 3D rendering (Owens et al. 2008; Hwu 2011). Neural networks have made matrix multiplication commercially dominant, driving the integration of two-dimensional systolic arrays and matrix execution engines (such as NVIDIA Tensor Cores and Google TPUs) directly into processor datapaths.

Owens, John D., Mike Houston, David Luebke, Simon Green, John E. Stone, and James C. Phillips. 2008. “GPU Computing.” Proceedings of the IEEE 96 (5): 879–99. https://doi.org/10.1109/jproc.2008.917757.
Hwu, Wen-mei W. 2011. “Introduction.” In GPU Computing Gems Emerald Edition. Elsevier. https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-12-384988-5.00064-4.

Linear algebra constitutes only part of the neural network execution pipeline. Between linear transformations, neural networks introduce nonlinear activation functions and normalization layers. While piecewise-linear functions such as ReLU map to simple vector comparison instructions, transcendental computations (such as exponentials in softmax and GELU, or reciprocal square roots in normalization) cannot be computed directly on multiply-accumulate datapaths without incurring severe cycle penalties. Table 3 summarizes the execution characteristics of the three primary compute primitives and their mapping to neural network operations.

11.3.3 Special function units

Standard multiply-accumulate hardware evaluates an exponential in softmax, a hyperbolic tangent in GELU, or a reciprocal square root in layer normalization only through a multi-instruction polynomial approximation, which can stall the pipeline between fast matrix kernels. Special Function Units (SFUs) and specialized instruction paths remove this bottleneck, completing the chapter’s trio of processing primitives. The need is not new: floating-point coprocessors addressed scalar arithmetic bottlenecks (Palmer 1980), and digital signal processors added specialized arithmetic for signal-processing workloads (Smith 1997). An implementation may use a standalone unit, vector approximation instructions, or a library sequence, trading accuracy, latency, and throughput. In neural networks, activation, normalization, and softmax operations can become the limiting stage between matrix kernels when repeated memory passes or transcendental functions cap throughput.

Palmer, John F. 1980. “The Intel 8087 Numeric Data Processor.” Proceedings of the 1980 National Computer Conference (AFIPS), 887–93. https://doi.org/10.1145/1500518.1500674.
Smith, Steven W. 1997. “Digital Signal Processing.” In Digital Signal Processing Demystified. Elsevier. https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-187870716-1/50004-4.

Nonlinear functions

A common layer sequence illustrates how non-matrix operators enter the execution pipeline (Goodfellow et al. 2016). Listing 8 chains a linear transformation with ReLU activation and batch normalization, operations that appear trivial in Python framework code but impose distinct arithmetic and memory constraints on hardware.

Goodfellow, Ian, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville. 2016. Deep Learning. MIT Press.

Listing 9 expands this sequence into its arithmetic primitives, isolating the element-wise thresholding of ReLU from the cross-batch reductions and reciprocal square root required by batch normalization. Here rows are samples and columns are features; weights has input features by output features, while bias, gamma, and beta contain one value per output feature. Keeping the reduced batch dimension permits those per-feature statistics to broadcast across samples.

Hardware implementation of nonlinear functions

Translating these mathematical functions to silicon exposes sharp differences in memory traffic, instruction count, and pipeline utilization. For instance, batch normalization (Ioffe and Szegedy 2015) demands multi-pass statistics gathering across memory, variance accumulation, and a reciprocal square root, while softmax requires computing exponentials across an entire normalization dimension. While a rectified linear unit (ReLU) is mathematically simple, a naive scalar implementation incurs branch overhead or redundant memory round-trips unless fused into adjacent kernels. Listing 10 contrasts the memory and dependency overheads of pointwise activation against multi-pass normalization in an unfused loop model.

Ioffe, Sergey, and Christian Szegedy. 2015. “Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift.” Proceedings of the 32nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 37: 448–56.

The label nonlinear hides three different execution patterns. Pointwise functions such as ReLU leave elements independent and therefore map naturally to vector lanes or parallel threads. Reductions such as the mean and variance in batch normalization introduce cross-element dependencies: partial results must be combined before later stages can proceed. Transcendental functions such as exponential, logarithm, and reciprocal square root add a numerical trade-off because their implementations balance latency, precision, and valid input range. The dependency pattern, not the mathematical label alone, determines whether vector arithmetic, a reduction tree, or a specialized approximation path is appropriate. A faster special-function path accelerates only the operation it implements; it does not remove surrounding tensor traffic or synchronization.

Listing 10 is intentionally dependency-explicit rather than a model of an optimized kernel. The loops expose three state lifetimes: per-element activations, per-feature accumulators, and the final normalized outputs. The normalization parameters cannot be applied until the required statistics are available, so implementations must either retain intermediate activations or recompute them. Training derives those statistics from the current batch, whereas inference can use stored statistics and reduce normalization to an element-wise affine transform. Compilers may fuse legal stages, but the data dependencies determine which transformations preserve the computation. Reading the listing as a dependency graph therefore reveals the durable hardware questions: how often each tensor crosses a memory interface, which intermediates remain local, and where reductions impose synchronization.

The dependency structure in listing 10 exposes two costs of naive execution. The pointwise ReLU and normalization scale-and-shift perform little arithmetic per accessed byte, so materializing each pass can place a low bandwidth ceiling on throughput. In this unfused loop model, temp is stored and reread after batch statistics are finalized; its physical traffic depends on cache residency and the chosen memory interface. Computing \(1/\sqrt{\text{var} + \NumericalStabilityConstant}\) also adds a dependent arithmetic path. The listing illustrates an iterative approximation, but actual kernels may use a reciprocal-square-root instruction and refinement, with device- and accuracy-dependent latency. Specialized function paths address this arithmetic cost, while legal fusion and local buffering reduce intermediate traffic. Neither removes the need to complete the reductions before normalization.

SFU hardware implementation

SFUs address arithmetic bottlenecks by implementing nonlinear and transcendental operations in specialized functional units rather than multi-instruction software routines. Accelerators deploy dedicated datapath circuits, such as quadratic polynomial interpolators and small lookup tables (LUTs), that evaluate functions like exponential, reciprocal square root, and logarithm within a few pipeline stages. Listing 11 illustrates how an instruction set exposes these operations alongside vector memory accesses.

Specialized function paths balance circuit area against mathematical precision. While piecewise linear activations such as ReLU require only single-cycle compare-and-select (maximum) datapath logic, transcendental functions trade off lookup table size and polynomial interpolation degrees against approximation error. Representative mechanisms and their qualitative latencies differ by function (table 4).

The two lighthouses use this path differently. ResNet-50 barely touches it: its only activation is ReLU, a comparison, and its only exponentials are the thousand in its final softmax. GPT-2 XL leans on it at every step, because each attention head applies softmax across the whole context and each feed-forward block applies GELU, so its special-function work grows with sequence length while ResNet-50’s stays fixed.

Vector operations, matrix operations, and special-function paths establish the foundational arithmetic primitives of ML accelerators, but functional units alone do not dictate sustained throughput. These primitives govern what the silicon computes; the execution model and memory hierarchy govern how data feeds the datapath. A matrix unit rated for hundreds of teraFLOP/s will idle if memory bandwidth cannot sustain operand delivery, if tile dimensions mismatch register blocking, or if thread synchronization serializes execution. Peak assumes operands are always ready; the execution model decides how much of it a real workload achieves.

    1. Systolic 2D Matrix Multiply Units

  5. Which of the following operations in a modern deep learning architecture exhibits the highest operational arithmetic reuse, making it most suitable for dense 2D systolic arrays and Tensor Cores?
