11.4 Compute Units

Applying ReLU to a 512-element vector shows why execution models matter. The operation is simple, but throughput depends on whether the hardware treats those 512 comparisons as scalar instructions, as lanes of a single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) unit, as GPU threads, or as tensor-program fragments. Modern AI processors package the three compute primitives into distinct execution units: vector units for vector work, matrix units such as Tensor Cores and systolic arrays for matrix work, and special function units for nonlinear functions. They then group those units into processing elements. That organization defines how computations are structured and exposed to programmers, and it explains why theoretical capability and delivered throughput diverge.

The packaging follows reuse per operand. For the reference low-precision operations, reading an operand from a register file and moving it across on-chip wires can cost more energy than the arithmetic itself, so each primitive goes to the unit whose dataflow supplies the reuse it offers. In D·A·M terms, this partition binds algorithmic primitives to machine execution paths. Routing dense matrix multiplications through vector pipelines saturates register-file read ports and collapses throughput to a small fraction of peak, while routing low-intensity elementwise work through matrix arrays leaves their lanes idle.

11.4.1 From SIMD lanes to SIMT threads

Even a wide CPU vector unit stalls when streaming through gigabytes of tensor data: cache misses freeze the pipeline for hundreds of cycles waiting on main memory, the instruction reorder buffer fills, and the SIMD lanes sit empty. The vector path of section 11.3.1 follows Flynn’s SIMD execution model, which amortizes instruction fetch and decode by issuing a single decoded instruction across multiple data elements packed into wide vector registers (Flynn 1966). A 512-bit SIMD register processes sixteen 32-bit floating-point values per instruction. The same idea appears in fixed-width CPU vector extensions, Arm’s length-agnostic Scalable Vector Extension (SVE) (Stephens et al. 2017), and two-dimensional tile extensions such as Intel’s Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) (Intel Corporation 2021a). Even so, those wide registers still live inside a CPU core built around branch predictors, out-of-order execution logic, and deep cache hierarchies for a few sequential threads. Conditional branching within a vector also requires evaluating divergent paths under bitmasks, further cutting useful lane utilization.

Flynn, M. J. 1966. “Very High-Speed Computing Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 54 (12): 1901–9. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1966.5273.
Stephens, Nigel, Stuart Biles, Matthias Boettcher, Jacob Eapen, Mbou Eyole, Giacomo Gabrielli, Matt Horsnell, et al. 2017. “The ARM Scalable Vector Extension.” IEEE Micro 37 (2): 26–39. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2017.35.
Lindholm, Erik, John Nickolls, Stuart Oberman, and John Montrym. 2008. “NVIDIA Tesla: A Unified Graphics and Computing Architecture.” IEEE Micro 28 (2): 39–55. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2008.31.
Nickolls, John, Ian Buck, Michael Garland, and Kevin Skadron. 2008. “Scalable Parallel Programming with CUDA: Is CUDA the Parallel Programming Model That Application Developers Have Been Waiting For?” Queue 6 (2): 40–53. https://doi.org/10.1145/1365490.1365500.

11 SM (streaming multiprocessor): The physical hardware engine that implements the SIMT model by using warp schedulers to coordinate many parallel threads. Maintaining enough active warps can help hide instruction and memory latency, but occupancy alone does not identify the bottleneck. Low occupancy may result from register use, shared-memory use, block dimensions, or insufficient parallel work, while a memory-bound kernel can still have high occupancy.

Architectures built on single instruction, multiple threads (SIMT) execution resolve these bottlenecks by decoupling the logical programming abstraction from physical hardware execution (Lindholm et al. 2008; Nickolls et al. 2008). Instead of requiring the programmer to pack data into explicit vector registers, SIMT exposes an execution model of independent scalar threads. In GPU architectures, each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)11 coordinates thousands of concurrent threads. Hardware warp schedulers group these threads into warps, the 32-thread scheduling groups (wavefronts in AMD architectures) whose granularity already set lane utilization in training kernels. Every thread in a warp executes a common instruction in lockstep across parallel ALUs. This lockstep execution introduces a constraint known as warp divergence. When threads within a single warp take different paths through a conditional branch, the hardware must execute both required paths sequentially, masking off the inactive lanes during each path. This serialization reduces useful lane utilization and increases execution time, which is why performance-critical ML kernels avoid divergent branching in favor of uniform or predicated control flow.

↩︎ Warps as the 32-thread unit in which GPUs schedule tensor kernels are established in Compute operations.

Rather than relying on large caches to reduce memory latency, GPUs hide latency through extensive thread-level concurrency. An SM statically partitions an on-chip register file across all active threads, eliminating context-saving overhead. When one warp stalls waiting hundreds of cycles for an off-chip memory fetch, the warp scheduler selects and issues instructions from another ready warp on the very next cycle. The baseline matrix multiplication kernel in listing 12 illustrates how this scalar thread model maps onto hardware. CUDA organizes a grid of threads into blocks: blockIdx locates a block in the grid, blockDim gives the block dimensions, and threadIdx locates a thread within that block. Multiplying a block coordinate by its dimension and adding the within-block coordinate gives the global row or column used by the listing.

In listing 12, the CUDA12 kernel assigns one output element C[row * N + col] to each thread. Adjacent threads in a warp share the same row index while having consecutive column indices (threadIdx.x). When threads fetch B[k * N + col], their memory requests target contiguous 4-byte floating-point addresses. The memory controller merges these 32 individual 4-byte loads into a single 128-byte coalesced memory transaction, maximizing DRAM bus efficiency. Concurrently, all threads in the warp read the identical element A[row * N + k], allowing the hardware to broadcast that single fetched value across all 32 lanes. However, this naive kernel runs into the arithmetic intensity law (principle 6). Because each inner-loop iteration performs only two floating-point operations while reloading operands from global memory without on-chip SRAM staging, the kernel remains severely memory bound. Furthermore, executing dense matrix multiplication on scalar SIMT ALUs requires one instruction fetch, decode, and issue cycle for every multiply-accumulate, saturating register file read ports. Overcoming this machine bottleneck requires moving beyond vector-of-scalars execution to specialized two-dimensional matrix units.

12 CUDA (compute unified device architecture): Released by NVIDIA in 2006, CUDA eliminated the need to disguise general-purpose computations as graphics operations, opening GPUs to scientific and ML workloads through a C-like programming model. The ecosystem it created (cuBLAS, cuDNN, TensorRT) constitutes a software ecosystem whose switching cost can lock the ML training stack to NVIDIA hardware: migrating away requires rewriting or replacing thousands of GPU-optimized kernels, a cost that often exceeds the hardware savings of competing platforms. This software lock-in, not raw silicon performance alone, helps explain why many large ML training stacks remain CUDA-centered.

11.4.2 Tensor Cores

For a single transformer attention head over a 2,048-token sequence with 64-dimensional embeddings, the \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\times \AttentionKeyMatrix^T\) product multiplies a \(2048{\times}64\) matrix by a \(64{\times}2048\) matrix. That is roughly 268.4M MACs, or 536.9 MFLOP when the multiply and add are counted separately. On a scalar processor executing one FLOP per cycle at 2 GHz, that single attention head would take 268.4 ms. Even on GPU SIMT lanes, issuing a separate scalar fused multiply-add for every element pair saturates instruction-issue bandwidth and register-file read ports. Dedicated matrix engines remove both bottlenecks by organizing work around multidimensional tiles and reusing fetched operands across many multiply-accumulate operations on chip. NVIDIA GPUs expose Tensor Cores, the reduced-precision matrix units13 that mixed-precision training was built to exploit, whereas Google TPUs use matrix units built around systolic arrays. Both execute tiled matrix multiplication and accumulation.14

13 Reduced-precision ML: Halving operand width halves the bytes per stored element and can support denser arithmetic, although realized throughput depends on the available datapath and kernel (Dally et al. 2021; Dally 2023). NVIDIA’s transition from Pascal P100 vector arithmetic to mixed-precision Tensor Cores in Volta V100 increased advertised peak FP16 throughput from about 21.2 to 125 TFLOP/s, roughly 6\(\times\) across those products (NVIDIA 2017). Precision selection must preserve numerical behavior and use an efficient supported path; the smallest format is not automatically the best one.

Dally, William J., Stephen W. Keckler, and David B. Kirk. 2021. “Evolution of the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU).” IEEE Micro 41 (6): 42–51. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2021.3113475.
Dally, Bill. 2023. “Hardware for Deep Learning.” 2023 IEEE Hot Chips 35 Symposium (HCS), 1–58. https://doi.org/10.1109/hcs59251.2023.10254716.

14 Tensor Core dimension alignment: NVIDIA Tensor Cores are most efficient when matrix dimensions are aligned to precision- and architecture-specific multiples, such as multiples of 8 or 16 for common FP16/BF16/INT8 paths. Modern cuBLAS and cuDNN can still use Tensor Cores for many nonaligned dimensions, but poorly aligned shapes may trigger less efficient kernels, require padding, or reduce effective throughput (NVIDIA 2024a; NVIDIA Corporation 2021). This is why model architects often choose embedding and channel dimensions such as 512 rather than 500 and why batch-size-1 inference may fail to reach peak Tensor Core utilization: alignment and arithmetic intensity jointly determine whether the hardware’s matrix engines stay full.

NVIDIA Corporation. 2021. NVIDIA cuDNN Developer Guide.

Assume, for illustration, that the Tensor Cores of a single streaming multiprocessor complete that 2,048-token attention head in 0.5 ms, an implied rate of about 1.1 TFLOP/s and a small slice of a full GPU’s tensor peak. The tiled path is then roughly 536.9× faster than the scalar baseline, and that speedup comes not from a higher clock frequency but from hardwiring tile-level data reuse into the execution datapath. Whether a workload reaches that rate depends on tile reuse, matrix shape, numeric precision, and memory delivery.

In NVIDIA Parallel Thread Execution (PTX), Tensor Core operations are invoked through warp-synchronous matrix instructions (mma.sync).15 The mnemonic encodes the tile geometry and data types: .m16n8k16 gives the tile dimensions (\(\GemmRowDimension=16, \GemmColumnDimension=8, \GemmInnerDimension=16\)), and the trailing types (.f32.f16.f16.f32) declare FP16 inputs accumulated into an FP32 destination. In listing 13, all 32 threads in a warp execute this single instruction collectively to compute the tile product \(\MatrixMultiplyDestination= \GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand+ \GemmOutputMatrix\).

15 Tensor Core: A single Tensor Core instruction executes a complete matrix-multiply-accumulate operation on a small tile of data using a dedicated hardware block (NVIDIA 2017; NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). This approach bypasses the overhead of fetching and scheduling dozens of individual arithmetic instructions on general-purpose CUDA cores. Because these blocks constitute a large fraction of a modern accelerator’s advertised tensor throughput, failing to use them can leave most of the chip’s theoretical peak unavailable to the workload.

NVIDIA. 2017. Training with Mixed Precision.

Here inputs \(\GemmLeftOperand\) (\(16{\times}16\)) and \(\GemmRightOperand\) (\(16{\times}8\)) are FP16, while accumulator \(\GemmOutputMatrix\) and destination \(\MatrixMultiplyDestination\) (\(16{\times}8\)) are FP32. The register operands in listing 13 represent the per-thread fragment held by each of the 32 threads in the warp rather than the entire matrix tile. Because each 32-bit GPU register packs two 16-bit FP16 values, a single thread’s four source registers {a0,a1,a2,a3} hold 8 FP16 elements of \(\GemmLeftOperand\), so all 32 threads together supply the \(32 \times 8 = 256\) elements of the \(16{\times}16\) tile. Similarly, {b0,b1} holds 4 FP16 elements per thread (\(32 \times 4 = 128\) elements for the \(16{\times}8\) tile \(\GemmRightOperand\)), and {c0,c1,c2,c3} holds four 32-bit FP32 accumulator elements per thread (\(32 \times 4 = 128\) elements for the \(16{\times}8\) tile \(\GemmOutputMatrix\)). A single warp instruction evaluates all \(16 \times 8 \times 16 = 2{,}048\) multiply-accumulate operations that would otherwise require 64 separate scalar fused multiply-add (fma) instructions per thread. This tile-level execution relieves two bottlenecks of conventional SIMT pipelines: instruction-issue bandwidth and register-file read-port contention. In scalar SIMT execution, every fma reads its source operands fresh from the register file, whereas the Tensor Core reads each thread’s register fragment once and reuses every fetched element across multiple inner-product steps inside the matrix datapath.

Design priorities determine how matrix engines appear in different processor families. GPU Tensor Cores preserve programmability while accelerating general-purpose deep learning kernels. TPU-style designs use large-scale matrix units arranged in systolic arrays to maximize sustained training throughput on dense tensor kernels. Mobile NPUs16 shrink the same idea into low-power inference blocks, while server CPUs add matrix instruction extensions (AMX-class tiles) for inference and mixed workloads. Each version keeps a different amount of flexibility in exchange for removing a different amount of data movement.

16 NPU (neural processing unit): Mobile NPUs achieve low-power inference by implementing common tensor operations in fixed-function or narrowly programmable hardware rather than as fully general GPU kernels. This architectural commitment can deliver large energy-efficiency gains for supported kernels, but it makes deployment dependent on operator coverage: unsupported functions must fall back to a CPU or GPU path that may be far less efficient for that workload (Sze et al. 2017).

Sze, Vivienne, Yu-Hsin Chen, Tien-Ju Yang, and Joel S. Emer. 2017. “Efficient Processing of Deep Neural Networks: A Tutorial and Survey.” Proceedings of the IEEE 105 (12): 2295–329. https://doi.org/10.1109/jproc.2017.2761740.

Tensor Cores also changed how each accelerator generation states its peak. Successive generations combined more matrix units with narrower formats (FP16, then INT8, FP8, and FP4) and, from Ampere onward, a structured-sparsity path. As a result, the headline rating rose by more than three orders of magnitude between 2012 and 2024 while measuring a different precision at almost every step (NVIDIA Corporation 2017, 2020a, 2024; Choquette 2023). A peak quoted without its precision and sparsity assumption therefore says little about a given workload. The generation-by-generation ratings, with their precision-specific peaks, bandwidths, and power limits, are collected with the other dated specifications in Master accelerator matrix. Whatever the format, a Tensor Core retires a tile per instruction only when its operands are already nearby, so accelerators never deploy matrix units on their own. The next level of the execution hierarchy exists to supply that proximity.

11.4.3 Processing elements

High-throughput matrix units cannot be fed directly from global memory: off-chip DRAM and even on-package HBM lack the bandwidth and low latency required to stream fresh operands into dense arithmetic arrays on every cycle. Accelerators resolve this bandwidth deficit by grouping Tensor Cores, vector units, and special function units alongside high-bandwidth register files and scratchpad SRAM inside modular processing elements (PEs). Staging operands inside the PE keeps data adjacent to the functional units, amortizing the latency and energy cost of external memory accesses across repeated arithmetic reuse. The term is used at two scales in this chapter. Here a PE is a tile or core that bundles several units with local memory, the role a streaming multiprocessor plays in a GPU and a core plays in a TPU. Inside a systolic array (section 11.4.4), a PE is a single multiply-accumulate cell in the grid.

Processing element design varies because each architecture chooses a different balance between compute density, local memory capacity, and interconnect distance. Graphcore’s Intelligence Processing Unit (IPU), for example, distributes computation across tiles backed by dedicated local SRAM (Graphcore 2020). Retaining an operand in one tile saves external traffic, but a consumer on another tile still requires an interconnect transfer. Local storage therefore shifts the mapping problem toward keeping repeated consumers close to their operands.

Graphcore. 2020. The Colossus MK2 IPU Processor.

Across these designs, the binding physical constraint is compute density versus data locality: silicon area dedicated to arithmetic units cannot simultaneously house SRAM storage or routing wires. Packing more execution units raises peak theoretical FLOP/s, but those units idle if memory bandwidth and routing channels cannot deliver operands. A processing element’s delivered efficiency therefore depends as much on its local memory hierarchy and interconnect strategy as on its raw arithmetic capability. Systolic arrays push this locality principle to its limit: rather than staging operands in a processing element’s local memory and fetching them again for each operation, they pass operands directly from one processing element to its neighbor.

11.4.4 Systolic arrays

Even when operands sit in local SRAM or registers, reading two inputs and writing a partial sum back to a central register file on every multiply-accumulate burns wire energy and port bandwidth that limit how many arithmetic cells a chip can pack. While Tensor Cores amortize register access across instruction-driven micro-tiles, systolic arrays remove intermediate register-file round-trips altogether by wiring hundreds or thousands of processing elements into two-dimensional spatial grids. In a classic 2D systolic array, data streams rhythmically through adjacent cells on regular clock cycles: inputs march horizontally, partial sums accumulate vertically, and stationary weights remain anchored in place. Because every value passed from one processing element to its immediate neighbor participates in an arithmetic operation without returning to a register file or SRAM buffer, nearest-neighbor wires replace memory reads. An operand loaded once at the array edge contributes to \(\SquareGemmDimension\) sequential multiply-accumulate steps across an \(\SquareGemmDimension \times \SquareGemmDimension\) grid, driving memory traffic down by an order of magnitude. Counting DRAM accesses per multiply-accumulate with and without neighbor-to-neighbor passing makes the saving concrete.

Napkin Math 11.1: The energy advantage of pulsing data

Scenario: The systolic architecture improves energy efficiency by keeping operands local as work pulses through the array; the “Systolic” (heartbeat) metaphor reflects this benefit of reusing operands locally. This worked model compares systolic dataflow with a naive implementation that streams every operand through DRAM:

  1. DRAM-streaming baseline: Loads \(\GemmLeftOperand\), \(\GemmRightOperand\), and the running \(\GemmOutputMatrix\), computes \(\GemmLeftOperand\times \GemmRightOperand+ \GemmOutputMatrix\), and writes \(\GemmOutputMatrix\) back without cache or register reuse.
    • Data movement: 3 loads + 1 write = 4 DRAM accesses (per operation).
    • Energy: ≈ 4 \(\times\) 640 pJ + 1 pJ (compute) = 2561 pJ/op.
  2. Systolic array (128 \(\times\) 128): Loads \(\GemmLeftOperand\) and \(\GemmRightOperand\) once at the edges. Data “pulses” through 128 processing elements.
    • Data movement: 2 loads per 128 operations = 0.016 DRAM accesses (per operation).
    • Energy: ≈ 0.016 \(\times\) 640 pJ + 1 pJ (compute) ≈ 11 pJ/op.

Systems insight: Under this deliberately naive DRAM-streaming baseline, the worked model gives the systolic array a 232.8× energy advantage. The ratio measures locality, not an inherent gap between vector and systolic arithmetic.

  • Concretely, a \(128{\times}128\) array can sustain 16,384 MACs/cycle with a large energy saving by pulsing data through processing elements instead of repeatedly loading it from DRAM (Horowitz 2014; Jouppi et al. 2023).
  • This locality lets dense arrays sustain many simultaneous MAC operations without paying a DRAM access for every operation.
  • Limitation: The comparison assumes no effective reuse in the baseline and full reuse across the array. Caches, register blocking, array underutilization, and other dataflows change the ratio substantially.

17 Systolic array: Kung and Leiserson used the term for arrays in which data advances through neighboring processing elements on a regular schedule (Kung and Leiserson 1979). Pipeline fill permits concurrent wavefronts and local reuse. The benefit depends on the stationary operand, tile, buffers, and utilization; it does not guarantee fixed DRAM savings. Irregular workloads and poorly aligned shapes remain a weaker fit because fill, drain, and idle elements consume capacity.

Kung, Hsiang Tsung, and Charles E Leiserson. 1979. “Systolic Arrays (for VLSI).” Sparse Matrix Proceedings 1978 1: 256–82.
Kung, H. T. 1982. “Why Systolic Architectures?” Computer 15 (1): 37–46. https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.1982.1653825.

Kung and Leiserson17 (Kung and Leiserson 1979) first introduced systolic arrays, formalizing their use in parallel computing architectures for efficient matrix operations (Kung 1982). Unlike general-purpose execution units, systolic arrays exploit spatial and temporal locality by reusing operands as they propagate through the grid. Google’s TPU exemplifies this architectural approach: in the TPU v4, a \(128{\times}128\) systolic array of multiply-accumulate units processes matrix operations by streaming data through the array in a pipelined manner (Jouppi et al. 2023). Figure 5 traces this 2D pipelined dataflow: a control unit stages operands into input FIFO buffers that stream activation data horizontally across the processing grid, while partial sums accumulate vertically down columns into the bottom adder-accumulator chain. Each processing element performs one multiply-accumulate per cycle and passes its operands to its neighbors, so a value loaded once is reused across an entire row or column rather than refetched from memory.

A 128 \(\times\) 128 systolic array capable of 16,384 operations per cycle requires a continuous operand stream to maintain utilization. On-chip buffers feed activations and weights to the array edges and are replenished from off-chip memory as needed; reuse within the array avoids fetching every operand from HBM each cycle. The TPU v4’s 1,200 GB/s HBM2 bandwidth helps sustain this stream, but off-chip bandwidth can still limit models whose working sets and reuse patterns exceed on-chip capacity.

Systems Perspective 11.1: Matching architecture to workload
Challenge: Systolic arrays must choose which operand to keep stationary in processing-element registers (weights, inputs, or partial sums), and that choice hard-codes the hardware’s preference for certain model types. Section 11.7.3 develops the three options as a general mapping decision.

No single accelerator architecture suits every workload. A chip optimized for weight-stationary dataflow (like early TPUs) excels at convolutional neural networks (CNNs), where filter weights are small and reused across many image patches. That same architecture stalls on large language model (LLM) autoregressive inference at batch size 1, where the entire weight matrix must be read from off-chip memory once per generated token with zero batch reuse. No choice of stationary operand recovers reuse that does not exist; the levers are batching, lower-precision weights, and memory bandwidth.

11.4.5 Numerics and sparsity on the datapath

Storing weights in INT8 or pruning half of them to zero shrinks a checkpoint on disk. If the accelerator lacks a datapath that multiplies narrow integers or skips zero weights in silicon, however, the runtime must unpack those weights back to dense floating point and executes no faster than the baseline. Number formats and structured sparsity patterns were defined in Model Compression; what turns them into wall-clock speedups—including the ResNet-50 INT8 profile—is the hardware datapath that executes them. Systolic arrays and Tensor Cores often provision higher multiply-accumulate capacity for narrower formats such as FP16, BF16, INT8, and FP8, while halving or quartering the bytes moved per value relative to FP32. That speedup is not automatic: it requires a supported kernel, matching input and accumulation formats, and enough parallel work to keep the narrower datapath full without hitting another bottleneck.

Precision trade-offs

Lower precision is not free, for the range-and-precision reasons that forced loss scaling in mixed-precision training and that Numerical formats compared format by format. FP16 trades dynamic range for significand bits, BF16 keeps FP32’s exponent range at the cost of precision, and INT8 has no exponent at all, so its usable range depends on scale, zero-point, and clipping choices. For the hardware designer, those numerical properties set the silicon cost of each datapath. A narrower format needs a smaller multiplier and moves fewer bytes, but accumulation usually stays wider, as the FP32 accumulator of the Tensor Core instruction in listing 13 shows, so part of the area saved in the multipliers is spent keeping sums accurate.

↩︎ The software side of mixed-precision training, including loss scaling, is established in Mixed-precision training.

Precision support is integrated into execution units and memory paths. SIMD and SIMT lanes may support several scalar formats, while Tensor Cores (section 11.4.2) and systolic units (section 11.4.4) expose architecture-specific input and accumulation combinations. Changing storage alone may reduce bytes without producing the advertised arithmetic speedup, because the model must select a kernel that uses the efficient path. Converting FP32 weights to INT8 cuts weight traffic by 4\(\times\). Whether that moves a kernel from bandwidth bound to compute bound depends on the operation’s original arithmetic intensity, the ridge point of the accelerator’s INT8 path, and the overhead of quantization and dequantization (equation 10.4). Tiling and dataflow, not precision itself, determine reuse, while conversion, scaling, or fallback overhead can offset part of the gain. A format is useful only when the kernel and numerical policy can employ it safely.

Mixed-precision computing

Modern AI accelerators support mixed-precision execution, in which different stages of one computation use different numerical formats. The training recipe (FP16 or BF16 multiplications with FP32 accumulation) (Micikevicius et al. 2018; Mellempudi et al. 2019) is developed in Mixed-precision training, and the inference recipe (INT8 or INT4 weights with selected activations kept wider) in Numerical Precision: Changing How Values Are Stored. The hardware’s part is to execute several formats side by side, with an accumulator wide enough for each.

Micikevicius, Paulius, Sharan Narang, Jonah Alben, Gregory Diamos, Erich Elsen, David Garcia, Boris Ginsburg, et al. 2018. “Mixed Precision Training.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
Mellempudi, Naveen, Sudarshan Srinivasan, Dipankar Das, and Bharat Kaul. 2019. “Mixed Precision Training with 8-Bit Floating Point.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1905.12334.
NVIDIA. 2020b. TensorFloat-32 in the A100 GPU Accelerates AI Training, HPC up to 20x.
NVIDIA Corporation. 2017. NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU Architecture. NVIDIA Whitepaper.
NVIDIA Corporation. 2018. NVIDIA Tesla T4 Tensor Core GPU. NVIDIA product documentation.

The shift toward precision diversity is evident in the evolution of AI hardware. Early architectures such as NVIDIA Volta provided Tensor Core support only for FP16, whereas later architectures, including Turing and Ampere, added integer formats and then TF32, a hybrid between FP32 and FP16, alongside BF16 (NVIDIA 2020b; NVIDIA Corporation 2017, 2018, 2020a). The generation-by-generation list of supported formats belongs with the other dated specifications in System Assumptions; the durable observation is the direction of the trend, toward more formats, each narrower than the last.

The precision format used in hardware design has cascading implications across the entire system. Reducing an operand from FP32 to FP16 halves its value bytes. When those values dominate traffic, the reduction can substantially lower movement energy; the full energy budget still includes access counts, arithmetic, and other device activity (Horowitz 2014). Simultaneously, Tensor Cores and systolic arrays can pack more lower-precision multiply-accumulate units into the same silicon area, raising peak throughput (Dally et al. 2021; Dally 2023). Lower-precision integer arithmetic also consumes less energy than FP32 in representative technology studies (Horowitz 2014), and the inference-focused TPU v1 was built around 8-bit multiply units (Jouppi et al. 2017). Reduced precision can therefore cut value traffic and raise the supported compute ceiling at the same time.

Kuzmin, Andrey, Mart Van Baalen, Yuwei Ren, Markus Nagel, Jorn Peters, and Tijmen Blankevoort. 2022. “FP8 Quantization: The Power of the Exponent.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 14651–62. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1065.
Micikevicius, Paulius, Dusan Stosic, Neil Burgess, Marius Cornea, Pradeep Dubey, Richard Grisenthwaite, Sangwon Ha, et al. 2022. “FP8 Formats for Deep Learning.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2209.05433.

Each narrower format raises the arithmetic ceiling again. The H100 advertises 989 TFLOP/s on its dense FP16 tensor path and 1,979 TFLOP/s on its FP8 path, an 8-bit floating-point format introduced for training and inference (Choquette 2023; Kuzmin et al. 2022; Micikevicius et al. 2022). NVIDIA’s Blackwell (B200) architecture extends this trajectory with an FP4 tensor datapath (a 4-bit floating-point format that, unlike INT4, spends some of its four bits on an exponent and so trades uniform spacing for range). The datapath is rated at up to 9 PFLOP/s dense or 18 PFLOP/s sparse peak throughput per chip (NVIDIA Corporation 2024). Reaching those theoretical ceilings requires numerical representations, kernel implementations, and sparsity patterns that align exactly with the specialized hardware paths. Narrower numerical formats expand the available design space, but numerical stability and dynamic range requirements dictate whether a workload can safely use FP4.

N:M structured sparsity mechanics

The sparse rating in that comparison depends on one more datapath feature, one that skips zeros only when they follow a fixed pattern. While unstructured pruning reduces model parameter counts, it rarely translates to hardware speedup because arbitrary nonzero placements destroy memory locality. Hardware accelerators resolve this with N:M structured sparsity,18 the pruning constraint from model compression that keeps exactly \(\StructuredSparsityNonzeroCount\) of every \(\StructuredSparsityGroupSize\) contiguous values along the reduction dimension nonzero, so memory access stays uniform and indexing predictable across parallel execution units.

18 N:M structured sparsity: The 2:4 ratio (50 percent density) used by NVIDIA’s Ampere Sparse Tensor Cores is a hardware-friendly compromise: every contiguous four-value group retains two nonzero values, preserving regular indexing while halving the dense value payload (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). At 2:4, the metadata overhead is compact enough to store alongside the weights without overwhelming the memory-traffic savings, which is the constraint that makes the advertised 2\(\times\) tensor-math throughput path plausible when kernels and model weights satisfy the pattern.

NVIDIA Corporation. 2020a. NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU Architecture. NVIDIA Whitepaper, V1.0.

↩︎ The N:M and 2:4 structured sparsity patterns and their compressed storage are established in Structured pruning.

Parallel hardware needs this regularity because of how sparse matrices are encoded. Classical formats such as Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) and Block Compressed Sparse Row (BSR) rely on auxiliary index arrays to locate nonzero entries, and the corresponding activation gathers can touch scattered addresses, reducing useful bytes per memory transaction. Varying numbers of nonzeros across rows also create load imbalance and divergent execution. Block sparsity groups retained values into larger dense tiles to restore regularity, at the cost of a more restrictive pruning pattern. In the block formats, a short list of nonzero block indices tells the hardware which tiles to fetch, so zero blocks are never read. Whether an indexed format saves bytes or time at a given sparsity, its break-even point, is derived in Storage and execution break-even. The datapath question here is how regular the retained values must be for parallel hardware to use them.

↪ The CSR storage format is collected for reference in Sparse matrix formats.

NVIDIA. 2020a. Accelerating Matrix Multiplication with Block Sparse Format and NVIDIA Tensor Cores.

NVIDIA’s Sparse Tensor Cores implement the 2:4 instance of the N:M pattern (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a; NVIDIA 2020a). Their input is the compressed 2:4 encoding, the two retained values of each group plus a 4-bit metadata tag (2 bits per value) recording their original positions. During execution, the memory hierarchy transfers only the compressed weights and their metadata, halving the weight-value payload while adding metadata traffic; total transferred bytes therefore fall by less than half before other overheads. Inside the Sparse Tensor Core datapath, the 4-bit metadata steers an internal multiplexer network that selects the matching two values from an uncompressed four-element activation vector. These selected activations and the two nonzero weights are then routed into a half-sized dot-product multiplier tree. Because the hardware computes only on the nonzeros while streaming compressed weights, this design doubles the peak arithmetic instruction throughput. The result is an advertised 2\(\times\) tensor-math speedup over dense operations when weights are fine-tuned to satisfy the pattern (figure 6).

The 2:4 pattern saves about half of the weight bytes and half of the multiplies, minus the metadata, so the reduced weight payload can lower traffic across HBM and on-chip SRAM. A roofline comparison must use consistent accounting: useful dense-equivalent operations can stay fixed while bytes decrease, whereas the count of physically executed sparse operations also decreases. Metadata and activation traffic remain in either traffic budget. Narrower values and skipped zeros therefore help when they reduce the bytes moved and keep the matrix engines fed. The ResNet-50 INT8 profile collects that benefit only on an execution path that supports both its format and its shapes. How fast such a path can possibly run follows from one division.

Dividing a model’s total operation count by peak arithmetic throughput produces an idealized lower bound on execution time, not a realistic inference latency. On the H100’s INT8 tensor path, dividing ResNet-50’s 8.2 GFLOP per inference by the 1,979 TOPS peak yields a floor of about 4 μs, against 8 μs at the FP16 peak. Real single-image ResNet-50 inference takes far longer than either floor. Part of that gap is kernel launch, synchronization, and host overhead that no roofline captures; part is memory traffic in low-intensity layers, because bandwidth has improved more slowly than tensor arithmetic throughput. That imbalance decides whether the advertised INT8 peak delivers high sustained utilization or sits largely idle on a given workload (Horowitz 2014; Gholami et al. 2024). Closing the gap requires the other half of the anatomy, the memory hierarchy that supplies the compute units.

Self-Check: Question

  1. In NVIDIA’s Ampere and Hopper architectures, how does 2:4 structured sparsity achieve an up to \(2\times\) dense-equivalent Tensor Core throughput path for supported matrix multiplication?

    1. Exactly two non-zero values are preserved in every contiguous four-element block, so the value payload is halved while compact metadata records positions and sparse Tensor Cores compute only on the retained values
    2. Every alternate row of the weight matrix is dropped completely, allowing the GPU to halve the grid launch dimensions
    3. Four separate threads simultaneously execute one scalar multiply-accumulate instruction in a single clock cycle
    4. Floating-point numbers are converted to 2-bit integers, quadrupling register file capacity

  2. Place the following steps in the correct execution sequence for processing a matrix multiplication on an accelerator with Sparse Tensor Cores using 2:4 structured sparsity:

  1. Fine-tune or prune the weight matrix to ensure exactly two non-zero values exist in every four-element contiguous group
  2. Sparse Tensor Cores load compressed weights and decode metadata to gather matching input activation elements
  3. Multiply non-zero weights by gathered activations and accumulate into output partial sums on the sparse path
  4. Compress the sparse weight matrix by storing only the non-zero values alongside metadata describing their positions

  1. What is the primary numerical difference between FP16 and BF16 as presented in this section?

    1. FP16 uses fewer total bits than BF16, so it always transfers less data
    2. BF16 has a wider exponent range, while FP16 has more fraction precision within the same 16-bit width
    3. FP16 is an integer format, whereas BF16 is floating point

11.5 Memory Systems

That gap between a 4 μs arithmetic floor and real inference latency opens whenever the memory subsystem cannot deliver weights and activations fast enough to keep the compute units busy. Modern accelerators provide hundreds of teraflops (or even petaflops) on low-precision tensor datapaths (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a, 2024; Choquette 2023), yet their arithmetic pipelines idle as soon as memory traffic saturates the bus. This is the memory wall, the growing divergence between arithmetic capability and memory bandwidth, seen from inside the accelerator.

↩︎ The memory wall, the widening gap between compute growth and memory bandwidth growth, is established in Physical Constraints on Deployment.

Because deep neural networks manipulate millions or billions of parameters across high-dimensional activation tensors, performance is frequently dictated by data movement rather than raw arithmetic capacity. Accelerators combat this memory wall through tiered storage hierarchies, software-managed scratchpads, high-bandwidth 3D stacked memory, and architectural dataflow strategies designed to maximize spatial and temporal reuse. For the chapter’s ResNet-50 workload the question becomes where each activation tile lives between the moment one convolution writes it and the moment the next consumes it, and what each tier on that path costs in time and energy.

11.5.1 The AI memory wall

Upgrading to an accelerator with twice the peak FLOP/s yields zero speedup when a workload’s weights and activations already saturate memory bandwidth, pinning execution time at \(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}\). On an accelerator the AI memory wall is chiefly this bandwidth ceiling, set by the parameter volumes and activation tensors of deep learning rather than by the single-access latency gap of the classic CPU formulation. Adding more memory capacity does not remove it either, because a model that fits comfortably in device memory still waits on the rate at which its bytes reach the compute units of section 11.4. The energy side of the wall was set out with the energy ladder in section 11.2.3: an off-chip DRAM access costs about 173× the energy of the FP32 multiply that consumes its operand (figure 4). The memory wall adds the time side of the same imbalance, which grows with every hardware generation.

Quantifying the compute-memory performance gap

Over the past two decades, peak computational capabilities have grown substantially faster than DRAM bandwidth (Gholami et al. 2024). This divergence stems from physical scaling constraints: while transistor scaling and dense systolic arrays multiply arithmetic throughput, memory bandwidth remains bounded by pin counts, package-substrate routing density, and interface signaling power. Representative high-end accelerators can deliver on the order of \(10^3\) TFLOP/s of peak tensor throughput (for example, NVIDIA H100 delivering 989 TFLOP/s in FP16 or 1,979 TFLOP/s in dense FP8) while providing approximately 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth (Choquette 2023). This implies that on the order of \(10^2\) FLOP of work per byte moved is required to fully use the compute, a threshold section 11.6.2 calls the ridge point and that exceeds the arithmetic intensity of many practical neural network workloads.

When a workload’s arithmetic intensity falls below this threshold, data transfer (\(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}\)) sets the larger of the two modeled time bounds. Accelerators attempt to tolerate memory latency (typically hundreds of clock cycles for off-chip DRAM) by maintaining thousands of concurrent execution threads and switching between active warps while memory requests remain in flight. However, when memory bandwidth saturates or when register pressure limits occupancy, the scheduler runs out of independent instructions to issue. Compute pipelines then stall, leaving high-throughput tensor cores idle while waiting for operands. Simultaneously, wide off-chip memory buses that cross capacitive printed circuit board traces and PHY interfaces consume a substantial fraction of the chip’s thermal design power (TDP), which directly constrains the energy budget available for arithmetic logic (Horowitz 2014; Sze et al. 2017).

The time gap and the energy ladder describe the same pressure from two sides: each byte fetched from DRAM costs more time relative to the arithmetic it feeds with every generation, on top of its energy cost. The TPU v1’s performance-per-watt advantage (example 11.1) came largely from minimizing that off-chip movement through systolic arrays and large on-chip SRAM (Jouppi et al. 2017). Whether a model can exploit such a design depends on the pattern of its memory accesses, which differs sharply among parameters, activations, and optimizer state.

Dubey, Abhimanyu, Abhinav Jauhri, Abhinav Pandey, Abhishek Kadian, et al. 2024. The Llama 3 Herd of Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.21783.
DeepSeek-AI. 2025. “Insights into DeepSeek-V3: Scaling Challenges and Reflections on Hardware for AI Architectures.” Proceedings of the 52nd Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 1731–45. https://doi.org/10.1145/3695053.3731412.

Hardware balance is the supply side of the memory wall; model size is the demand side. The structural widening between model footprints and available memory bandwidth is what turns the iron law’s memory term into the binding constraint across generations. Parameter count is a capacity quantity. In low-batch dense decoding with weights streamed from device memory, weight traffic per generated token grows with the parameter count. Sparse expert models read selected experts rather than every stored parameter, so their total parameter counts do not directly specify per-token traffic. Figure 7 plots this logarithmic divergence relative to 2014. It contrasts the roughly 3,900× increase in dense model parameters (filled red points) against the 33× increase in per-device accelerator memory bandwidth (blue points). The contrast isolates the widening shaded memory-wall gap (Krizhevsky et al. 2012; Simonyan and Zisserman 2015; Brown et al. 2020; Chowdhery et al. 2022; Dubey et al. 2024). DeepSeek-V3 appears as an open marker at its total parameter count and is left out of the trend for exactly that reason (DeepSeek-AI 2025). Even high-bandwidth accelerators such as NVIDIA B200 and AMD MI300X/MI325X cannot close this growth-rate gap through bandwidth scaling alone (NVIDIA Corporation 2024; AMD 2023). Parameter counts for proprietary systems such as GPT-4 and Gemini are not officially disclosed, so they are not plotted as factual data points.

11.5.2 Memory access patterns in ML workloads

In dense FP16 autoregressive generation at batch size 1, streaming a model’s weights from device memory for each generated token yields roughly 1 FLOP/byte on the matrix-vector work, starving compute units before activations or gradients ever enter the picture. Across training and inference, parameters, activations, and optimizer states compete for that same memory bandwidth in distinct ways. Model parameters (weights and biases) can span hundreds of billions of values (Brown et al. 2020) that must stream from memory whenever batch reuse is low. Intermediate activations produced at each layer must also be buffered for subsequent operations, and during training those forward activations must either stay in memory until backpropagation consumes them or be recomputed on the backward pass. Training then compounds the traffic with gradients and optimizer state. Backpropagation writes a gradient for every parameter, and adaptive optimizers such as Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) read and write multi-word momentum states on every step, multiplying the bytes moved per parameter update (Narayanan et al. 2021; Kwon and Rhu 2018).

Brown, Tom B., Benjamin Mann, Nick Ryder, Melanie Subbiah, Jared Kaplan, Prafulla Dhariwal, Arvind Neelakantan, et al. 2020. “Language Models Are Few-Shot Learners.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33: 1877–901. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2005.14165.
Kwon, Youngeun, and Minsoo Rhu. 2018. “TensorDIMM: A Practical Near-Memory Processing Architecture for Embeddings and Tensor Operations in Deep Learning.” Proceedings of the 52nd Annual IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture, 740–53. https://doi.org/10.1145/3352460.3358284.

The physical cost of this data movement depends on where each tensor resides in the memory hierarchy. While an on-chip register access completes in a single clock cycle at sub-picojoule energy, a dependent off-chip DRAM fetch can expose hundreds of cycles of latency and expends orders of magnitude more energy. Independent requests can overlap that latency, subject to available concurrency and bandwidth. Tracing a single tensor of the chapter’s ResNet-50 workload through the memory tiers during an inference pass makes this disparity concrete (lighthouse 11.2).

Lighthouse 11.2: Life of a tensor: A ResNet-50 activation map
Follow one activation map of the chapter’s ResNet-50 workload, the output of a stage-2 convolution (\(56{\times}56\) positions by 64 channels), on its way to the next convolution’s Tensor Cores on an H100:

  1. HBM: The previous kernel wrote the map here.
    • Size: 201 KB per image at INT8 and 401 KB at FP16; a batch of 32 holds 6.4 MB at INT8.
    • Latency: A dependent off-chip request takes about 273 ns, while streaming one image’s map at full bandwidth would take only about 60 ns, so the kernel must keep many requests in flight to approach the bandwidth ceiling.
    • Energy: About 160 pJ per byte in the 45 nm estimates used throughout the chapter, or about 32.1 µJ to read one image’s map once.
  2. L2 cache: The H100 shares 50 MB of L2 across its streaming multiprocessors (SMs), enough to hold the whole batch’s map at INT8 if the next kernel consumes it soon after the previous one wrote it.
    • Latency: About 150 ns on Hopper.
  3. Shared memory: One SM stages a tile of the map in its 228 KB of software-managed shared memory. A whole image’s map fits at INT8 but not at FP16, so the INT8 format changes which tier can hold it.
    • Latency: About 17 ns on Hopper.
  4. Registers: The Tensor Core reads its operands here.
    • Latency: A small number of cycles, depending on the instruction.
    • Energy: About 0.1 pJ per access, more than three orders of magnitude below an off-chip access.
    • Device arithmetic peak: 1,979 TOPS on the H100 INT8 tensor path, the rate these registers must sustain, not a register-transfer rate.

Systems insight: Latency and energy per access rise from registers to HBM. The working set’s location, access count, reuse, and dependencies determine the memory contribution to time and energy; arithmetic adds its own cost. The bandwidth term of the roofline is whichever link of this ladder the working set must cross; HBM-to-L2 is one possible limiting link, not the only one.

The boundary between bandwidth-bound and compute-bound execution emerges directly from the balance between data transfer time and arithmetic execution time. Consider a workload that requires data volume \(\DataVolume\) (bytes) across available memory bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\) (bytes/s). It executes \(\Operations\) floating-point operations on hardware with peak throughput \(\PeakRate\) (FLOP/s) at realized hardware utilization \(\EfficiencyHw\). The respective execution times are the iron law’s data and compute terms: \[\begin{gather*} \IronlawTermTimesMemory = \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} \\ \IronlawTermTimesCompute = \frac{O}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} \end{gather*}\]

In a strictly sequential model without overlap, \(\IronLawMemoryTime > \IronLawComputeTime\) identifies bandwidth-bound execution. When hardware overlaps memory transfers with computation, the larger term sets the theoretical lower bound on execution time. In practice, however, data dependencies, memory controller queueing, and partial pipeline overlap dictate how much arithmetic hardware remains idle while waiting for operands.

Irregular memory access

Production machine learning workloads combine regular dense matrix kernels with irregular memory access patterns that defeat conventional caching and prefetching hardware. While dense operations like general matrix multiply (GEMM) and convolution stream contiguous blocks that map cleanly onto hardware caches and systolic arrays, irregular operations rely on indirect, sparse, or input-dependent memory addresses. Table 5 contrasts these two memory regimes across access geometry, cache locality, and hardware pressure.

Within a single neural network, memory access behavior varies sharply across layer types. Convolutional layers have high spatial locality and register reuse as small weight kernels slide across input feature maps. Fully connected layers and dense attention, by contrast, execute regular matrix multiplications whose large parameter matrices or key-value caches can exceed on-chip SRAM capacity and become bandwidth bound when operational reuse is low. Variable sequence lengths complicate memory buffer allocation, yet the attention operations within each sequence remain regular, contiguous matrix multiplies.

True memory irregularity arises instead from unstructured sparsity,19 embedding lookups, and dynamic token routing. Unstructured sparsity stores nonzero weights or activations in compressed formats (such as CSR or COO) that require pointer indirection to decode operand coordinates. Embedding tables break sequential transfers in a different way: sparse categorical IDs select arbitrary rows from tables spanning tens of gigabytes in DRAM, turning reads into uncoalesced, scattered fetches. DLRM, the book’s capacity-bound lighthouse, is the extreme case. Its embedding tables exceed one accelerator’s memory, and each lookup fetches a short row from an address known only when the input arrives, which defeats both caches and prefetchers. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models introduce a third irregularity at the routing layer, where gates direct tokens to different expert networks based on input context. Although deterministic for a given input, token assignments vary across batches, disrupting prefetch pipelines and unbalancing execution queues across parallel cores.

19 Sparsity and memory irregularity: Unstructured sparse formats commonly gather nonzero elements through indirect addressing, which can weaken sequential access and make metadata overhead significant. Structured sparsity preserves hardware-friendly blocks, so its access behavior differs from arbitrary pruning. Without suitable kernels or hardware support, an unstructured sparse model can run slower than its dense counterpart despite performing fewer arithmetic operations.

Irregularity degrades performance through distinct mechanisms, and treating them as one memory problem can point to the wrong optimization. Scattered addresses may turn one logical access into several memory transactions, so each fetched cache line carries few useful payload bytes. Indirection can also serialize address generation: the system must fetch an index or pointer before it knows which payload to request, limiting memory-level parallelism even when aggregate bandwidth remains available. Input-dependent routing creates a third failure mode when some processing elements receive longer queues than others; completion time follows the slowest queue while neighboring units idle. Variable-sized allocations may fragment capacity, but fragmentation is neither necessary nor sufficient for irregular access. A sequential stream can saturate bandwidth without being irregular, whereas a dependent lookup chain can stall far below peak bandwidth.

The paired address strips in figure 8 isolate spatial utilization from address dependence. The example counts traffic at a declared sector interface, so it does not infer physical DRAM traffic from logical addresses alone.

Packing requests into fewer sectors reduces surplus bytes at that interface. It does not remove the dependency in the lower panel: the payload request still waits until the index or pointer returns its address. Increasing bandwidth and exposing independent requests therefore address different limits.

Diagnosis should therefore begin with the mechanism that prevents forward progress. A low ratio of useful payload bytes to transferred bytes indicates poor spatial utilization or coalescing. Long memory stalls alongside unused bandwidth indicate dependent misses or too few concurrent requests to hide latency. Uneven queue depths or per-route work reveal load imbalance rather than a cache-capacity problem. Cache hit rate alone cannot distinguish these cases because a miss can waste bandwidth, expose latency, or both. Each diagnosis implies a different remedy: packing or blocking improves spatial utilization, reordering and prefetching expose concurrent requests, structured sparse formats reduce indexing overhead, and routing or partitioning balances work. The memory hierarchy determines the cost of the remaining accesses, while dataflow and tensor-layout choices determine how much irregularity software can remove before execution reaches the hardware.

The optimization order follows that diagnosis. Representation comes first when the format is under system control because a block-structured sparse format or grouped routing can remove indirection before a kernel executes. Request organization comes next: accesses issued together should target adjacent addresses, and enough independent requests must remain in flight to hide unavoidable latency. Additional cache capacity or bandwidth helps only when profiling shows that the regularized request stream still exhausts that resource. More bandwidth cannot resolve a serial pointer dependency, and more capacity cannot rebalance skewed work. The objective is to expose as much regular structure as possible while confining unavoidable irregularity to the smallest portion of execution.

Software can mitigate irregular access by regularizing tensor layouts, enforcing structured sparsity, and sorting dynamic routes into uniform batches. Yet software restructuring cannot eliminate the physical penalty of data movement: whether a memory request is contiguous or scattered, every transferred byte must cross physical wires governed by finite bandwidth, propagation latency, and energy dissipation. Bounding these physical costs requires organizing storage into cascading hardware tiers. Rather than treating memory as a uniform pool, accelerator architectures deploy multilevel memory hierarchies that trade off capacity against latency and energy at every tier.

11.5.3 Memory hierarchy

No single storage technology can simultaneously satisfy the multi-terabyte-per-second bandwidth required by dense execution units and the tens of gigabytes of capacity required to hold modern model parameters. Accelerators resolve this tension through multilevel memory hierarchies. Rather than treating memory as a monolithic address space, the machine organizes storage into distinct physical tiers, each optimized for a specific balance of capacity, access latency, bandwidth, and energy dissipation.

At the apex of the hierarchy, register files and on-chip SRAM caches supply operands to arithmetic units with sub-nanosecond latency and single-digit picojoule energy costs, but their capacity is strictly limited by silicon die area. At the base, nonvolatile flash storage holds hundreds of gigabytes of model checkpoints and training datasets, but requires milliseconds or microseconds to access. Between these boundaries, software-managed scratchpads stage active tensor tiles, while device-local DRAM (such as HBM or GDDR) provides the primary working memory for parameters and activations.

This organization establishes an inverse relationship across tiers: as storage capacity expands and physical distance from arithmetic units grows, bandwidth falls, latency lengthens by orders of magnitude, and energy consumption per bit escalates. Table 6 compares these tiers across latency, bandwidth, capacity, and functional roles in deep learning workloads.

A recurring systems question is why accelerators cannot bypass on-chip SRAM entirely and stream all operands directly from high-capacity off-chip DRAM. A dependent DRAM request exposes the full access latency. Many independent requests can hide that latency, but their sustained operand supply remains limited by off-chip bandwidth; on-chip staging also enables reuse.

Napkin Math 11.2: Why HBM cannot feed the array directly
Problem: Why is on-chip SRAM necessary instead of fetching all data from HBM?

Math:

  1. Clock cycle: At 2 GHz, \(1/(2\text{ GHz}) = 500\text{ ps}\).
  2. DRAM access: Off-chip HBM sits millimeters away on the package, but row activation, DRAM-array latency, serialization, protocol traversal, and queuing add up to 100+ cycles per access.
  3. Distance, for comparison: On an H100-class 814 mm² die, signals travel ~20 mm; at \(\approx 0.5\VacuumLightSpeed\), \(20\text{ mm}/(0.5\VacuumLightSpeed) \approx 130\text{ ps}\), less than one cycle.

Systems insight: The propagation estimate alone does not explain the DRAM access cost, and it omits real interconnect delay from wiring and routing. Independent requests can overlap the 100-plus-cycle access path; a dependent request cannot. Registers and SRAM supply operands at the rate the array needs while reusing values that would otherwise cross HBM repeatedly. Transformer tiling addresses both operand supply and reuse, whereas streaming a growing KV cache can still limit inference when its required traffic exceeds the available bandwidth.

On-chip memory

The on-chip memory subsystem integrates registers, Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM) caches, and software-managed scratchpads directly on the accelerator die. Register files provide the immediate operand and accumulator storage needed by execution pipelines. Modern accelerators provision substantial register capacity in aggregate across the chip, but partition this pool dynamically among concurrent threads or warps. Increasing per-thread register allocation allows individual threads to retain larger matrix tiles, but limits the total number of concurrently scheduled warps, reducing the hardware’s ability to hide memory latency. Conversely, underallocating registers forces the compiler to spill values to off-chip memory, converting single-cycle register accesses into multi-cycle stalls. Efficient kernel design balances register allocation to maintain maximum occupancy while keeping hot operands resident.

Hardware-managed L1 and L2 caches provide fast buffering for frequently referenced data using automatic tag checking and hardware eviction policies. However, automatic caches are poorly suited for streaming multi-gigabyte tensor operations: scanning through large activation tensors can evict reusable weight tiles before arithmetic units can reuse them. Furthermore, specialized execution pipelines impose strict layout and data-type constraints that general caches cannot satisfy automatically. As illustrated in example 11.3, hardware matrix engines require specific alignments and memory layouts; a mismatch may require padding, conversion, or a different kernel whose efficiency must be checked.

Example 11.3: Tensor Cores that never engage
Scenario: An engineering team migrates a transformer workload to NVIDIA A100 GPUs expecting automatic Tensor Core acceleration, but profiling reveals Tensor Cores remain idle (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a).

Diagnosis: The workload used shapes and data types that selected less efficient kernels rather than the intended Tensor Core path.

Systems lesson: Specialized paths have operator, precision, layout, and shape requirements. Libraries can often handle nonaligned dimensions through padding or alternative kernels, but reaching high utilization requires verifying which path was actually selected.

To avoid the eviction overhead and unpredictability of automatic caches, AI accelerators incorporate scratchpad memory. Unlike hardware caches, scratchpads are software-managed SRAM structures mapped directly into the core’s address space without tag directories or hardware replacement logic. The compiler or programmer explicitly controls when tensor tiles are loaded from external DRAM, how long they reside on-chip, and when updated values are written back. In convolutional models, scratchpads retain input feature maps and weight kernels across sliding receptive windows, eliminating redundant DRAM reads (Chen et al. 2017). On NVIDIA GPUs, scratchpad memory is exposed as shared memory: a fast, programmer-controlled SRAM bank shared across all threads within a thread block. Custom kernels written in CUDA or Triton manage shared memory explicitly. FlashAttention demonstrates the power of this mechanism. Rather than materializing the full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) attention score matrix in off-chip HBM, the kernel tiles queries, keys, and values through shared memory and updates softmax statistics online (Dao et al. 2022). The speedup stems entirely from eliminating high-latency HBM round trips rather than reducing arithmetic operations; in fact, the algorithm recomputes intermediate attention values during the backward pass to avoid storing them to off-chip memory.

↩︎ FlashAttention as an IO-aware attention kernel for training is established in FlashAttention: IO-aware attention optimization.

Off-chip memory

When tensor working sets exceed on-chip SRAM capacity, operands and parameters reside in device-local DRAM. Rather than sequential hierarchy levels, HBM, Graphics DDR (GDDR), and Low-Power DDR (LPDDR) represent alternative memory architectures engineered for distinct cost, bandwidth, and power envelopes. High-performance accelerators use HBM, which stacks DRAM dies vertically using through-silicon vias (TSVs) and interfaces with the accelerator die across a wide silicon interposer (e.g., 1,024 to 8,192 bits). This wide bus delivers multi-terabyte-per-second bandwidth at lower clock frequencies and lower energy per bit than conventional DRAM, but requires complex 2.5D packaging. Where silicon interposers are cost-prohibitive, accelerators adopt GDDR, which uses narrower buses (e.g., 256 to 384 bits) driven at high pin speeds across standard circuit boards. Mobile and embedded accelerators use LPDDR, trading raw bandwidth for low operating voltage and reduced standby power.

When parameter and activation footprints exceed device-local DRAM capacity, the system must offload state to host DRAM (typically standard DDR). Accessing host memory requires crossing an I/O interconnect such as PCIe or a coherent fabric like NVLink or Compute Express Link (CXL). Because PCIe bandwidth (tens of gigabytes per second) is one to two orders of magnitude lower than accelerator DRAM bandwidth, unmanaged offloading stalls arithmetic execution. Efficient runtimes mitigate this penalty by overlapping asynchronous direct memory access (DMA) copies with kernel execution, prefetching upcoming layer parameters while current layers compute.

At the base of the hierarchy, nonvolatile flash storage and solid-state drives (SSDs) provide persistent, multi-terabyte capacity for datasets and training checkpoints (Narayanan et al. 2021). With read latencies measured in tens of microseconds and bus bandwidths capped at single-digit gigabytes per second, flash devices cannot participate directly in kernel execution. Checkpointing and data-loading pipelines treat flash storage as an asynchronous streaming source, staging batches through host DRAM into accelerator memory before computation begins.

Narayanan, Deepak, Mohammad Shoeybi, Jared Casper, Patrick LeGresley, Mostofa Patwary, Vijay Korthikanti, Dmitri Vainbrand, et al. 2021. “Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM.” Proceedings of the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis, 1–15. https://doi.org/10.1145/3458817.3476209.

The physical tiers of the memory hierarchy establish the latency floors and capacity ceilings of the accelerator, but advertised memory bandwidth is only a ceiling within them. Achievable bandwidth depends on access pattern, batching, locality, and the host interface that feeds the accelerator. Peak figures assume continuous, stride-1 coalesced access across all memory channels. Real neural network workloads deviate substantially from this ideal: transformer attention, convolution, and fully connected layers realize distinct fractions of peak bandwidth because their memory access strides, tiling dimensions, and operational reuse differ. A sufficiently large, coalesced weight stream can approach peak bandwidth even at small batch size. Batching instead reuses each loaded weight across more samples, raising arithmetic intensity as analyzed under the roofline model in section 11.6. Small or irregular kernels may lack enough concurrent accesses to approach the bandwidth ceiling, making memory latency and available parallelism part of the diagnosis.

11.5.4 Host-accelerator communication

An accelerator rated for hundreds of teraflops sits idle if its input tensors are still crawling across a host PCIe bus an order of magnitude slower than its on-package HBM. In discrete accelerator systems, the host CPU and the accelerator operate as separate computational domains joined by a peripheral bus. The host manages storage I/O, network streams, and runtime orchestration in system DRAM, while the accelerator executes dense mathematical kernels over device memory (HBM or GDDR). Because those two memories occupy separate physical address spaces, computation cannot begin until tensors cross the host-accelerator interconnect, making peripheral bus bandwidth and launch latency a hard gate on end-to-end speedup.

Figure 9 sequences the four-stage execution trace across host and device lifelines. Step 1 copies input data across PCIe to device memory via DMA. Step 2 dispatches kernel instructions from the CPU. Step 3 executes parallel core compute with local writeback. Step 4 copies results back to host memory. In a naive synchronous execution model, every transfer step sits directly on the critical path, stalling either the host or the accelerator until each memory transaction finishes.

The end-to-end latency of a kernel launch decomposes into transfer time, queue dispatch overhead, and arithmetic execution time. When tensor transfers are small or frequent, the fixed overhead of driver submission and bus round trips dominates runtime. When transfers are large, the low bandwidth of PCIe relative to on-package HBM creates a sustained I/O bottleneck. In D·A·M terms, the Machine boundary between host and accelerator forces the Algorithm to maximize arithmetic reuse on the device once tensors arrive.

Node-level interconnect topology

Within a single machine, how bits move between GPUs and the CPU sets the next ceiling. In the 1–8 GPU regime, scaling is achieved through high-speed intra-node interconnects such as NVLink and host-to-device PCIe transfers that mitigate the memory wall. These links form a bandwidth taper: data-movement speed falls at each step away from the compute units, from on-package HBM through the GPU-to-GPU NVLink bridge down to the host PCIe link. The PCIe step is much slower than the accelerator-local memory and inter-GPU fabric, so any data path that touches the CPU can become a performance hazard. Keeping accelerator-to-accelerator traffic off that link is the reason NVLink exists (NVIDIA Corporation 2020b). A typical AI server is therefore not a flat mesh of connected devices, and optimizing data movement starts from its physical topology.

Bandwidth tapers steeply as data moves farther from the accelerator.

Within a multi-accelerator server node, two interconnect tiers define this bandwidth taper below device memory:

  1. Device-device interconnect (NVLink/Infinity Fabric): Modern multi-GPU nodes use specialized high-speed bridges like NVLink20 to connect accelerators directly, bypassing the host CPU. Bandwidth ranges from 600 GB/s to 900 GB/s per GPU (NVIDIA Corporation 2020b; Choquette 2023). This link matters whenever tensors must move between accelerators within one server, including model partitioning, activation exchange, and gradient synchronization during training. The architectural principle is the boundary: traffic that stays on the accelerator fabric is far cheaper than traffic that falls back through the host.
  2. Host-device interconnect (PCIe): The link between the CPU and the accelerator. Bandwidth ranges from 32 to 64 GB/s (PCIe Gen4/Gen5). Host-staged training data can bottleneck here, although resident data, direct storage or network I/O, and coherent accelerator links can use other paths. Multi-GPU servers may also provide multiple PCIe links rather than a single shared 64 GB/s path.

20 NVLink (NVIDIA Link): This direct GPU-to-GPU interconnect exists to keep accelerator-to-accelerator traffic off PCIe when tensors must move inside a server. Its 600–900 GB/s aggregate bidirectional bandwidth is roughly 300–450 GB/s per direction under balanced full-duplex traffic, several times the directional bandwidth of a standard PCIe link, so workloads with frequent cross-device tensor movement can remain in the fast part of the bandwidth taper (NVIDIA Corporation 2020b; Choquette 2023). Training algorithms determine how much tensor traffic must cross this link; the hardware fact needed here is the bandwidth gap.

NVIDIA Corporation. 2020b. “NVLink: Scalable High-Performance Interconnect.” NVIDIA Technical Report 2020.
Choquette, Jack. 2023. “NVIDIA Hopper H100 GPU: Scaling Performance.” IEEE Micro 43 (3): 9–17. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2023.3256796.

A third tier, the network link from one server to others, continues the taper beyond the node (section 11.9). Together the levels produce a characteristic bandwidth taper:

\[\begin{aligned} \text{HBM (3350 GB/s)} &\gg \text{NVLink (900 GB/s)} \\ &\gg \text{PCIe (64 GB/s)} > \text{Network (50 GB/s)} \end{aligned}\]

System efficiency depends on keeping tensors on the highest-bandwidth links available. Because PCIe and network links offer orders of magnitude less bandwidth and higher latency than on-package memory, placement and scheduling must minimize crossings across these boundaries.

Transfer optimization

The standard remedy for transfer overhead is the asynchronous pipeline of Devices and memory. Batches staged in pinned (page-locked) host memory are copied by dedicated DMA engines while the accelerator computes on the previous batch. This double buffering conceals transfer latency behind arithmetic runtime whenever computation time exceeds transfer time (\(\IronLawComputeTime \ge \BatchTransferTime\)). When compute duration is too short to amortize the transfer, execution remains bus bound and the compute units stall.

↩︎ The feeding problem, in which data delivery fails to keep pace with compute throughput, is established in The feeding problem.

Unified Memory takes the opposite approach, presenting a single virtual address space that spans host DRAM and device HBM while the driver migrates pages on demand whenever either processor touches an address. On-demand migration removes staging code at the cost of predictability, because each page fault stalls execution and scattered accesses can thrash pages across the PCIe bus. High-throughput production workloads therefore rely on explicit, pipelined DMA transfers and reserve Unified Memory for prototyping or for applications where programmer productivity outweighs sustained hardware utilization. Once tensors reside on the accelerator, the model’s own architecture determines whether weights, activations, or lookup tables dominate the device memory hierarchy.

11.5.5 Model memory pressure

An optimization that relieves memory pressure for one model family can leave another untouched: caching weights helps nothing when ResNet-50’s early convolutions spill large activation maps to DRAM, and spatial activation tiling helps nothing when GPT-2 decode streams gigabytes of weights for a single token. Model architecture determines which memory term binds. The architectural reasons each family stresses memory as it does were traced in Arithmetic intensity across workloads; the hardware consequence differs by family, and the lighthouse models of Lighthouse Models as Reference Workloads cover the cases.

Dense layers, the multilayer perceptron (MLP) blocks that every family contains, are bound by weight traffic at small batch. At batch size \(\BatchSize= 1\), each parameter loaded from off-chip memory serves a single multiply-accumulate operation (often \(\le 1\text{ FLOP/byte}\)), so execution sits on the bandwidth slope; batching reuses each loaded weight across \(\BatchSize\) inputs and moves the layer toward the compute ceiling. Dense weight matrices regularly exceed the tens of megabytes of on-chip SRAM, so parameters reside in HBM and stream through tiles that the accelerator double-buffers into SRAM (Chen et al. 2017). The host link enters the critical path only when inputs stream from the host or when the model exceeds device memory.

Chen, Yu-Hsin, Joel Emer, and Vivienne Sze. 2017. “Using Dataflow to Optimize Energy Efficiency of Deep Neural Network Accelerators.” IEEE Micro 37 (3): 12–21. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2017.54.

Convolutional layers, the core of ResNet-50, place their memory pressure on activations rather than weights. Small filters sliding across feature maps supply three forms of reuse: neighboring windows share input activations, each filter is applied at every spatial position, and each input channel feeds every output filter. Early layers therefore carry compact parameter tensors but large activation maps that exceed on-chip SRAM, and unoptimized layer-by-layer execution spills those maps to device DRAM. Spatial tiling keeps activation tiles, with their overlapping boundary pixels, in on-chip buffers so adjacent convolutions consume them without refetching (Chen et al. 2017).

Transformers such as GPT-2 stress both capacity and bandwidth, differently in each phase. During training and prefill, standard attention materializes an \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) score matrix for sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) and moves \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) bytes through HBM; IO-aware kernels such as FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022) keep those tiles in on-chip SRAM instead (FlashAttention: IO-aware attention optimization). During autoregressive decode, each generated token reads the weights and the accumulated key-value (KV) cache from HBM for a vector-matrix product, which binds generation speed to memory bandwidth.

↩︎ How much memory one request’s KV cache claims as its sequence grows is established in Autoregressive decoding.

Two other lighthouses stress memory in other ways. DLRM’s sparse embedding lookups stress random-access bandwidth rather than dense compute, and MobileNetV2’s depthwise convolutions trade arithmetic intensity for a smaller parameter footprint, so both reappear as memory-bound rows in the roofline operations table (table 7). Accelerators answer these divergent demands with the tiered hierarchy. On-chip SRAM captures high-reuse activations and tiled matrix blocks at tens of terabytes per second, HBM stages large weight tensors and sequence state, and NVLink-class links carry tensors between accelerators when a model exceeds one device, avoiding the narrower host PCIe bus. Table 14 later pairs each family’s memory profile with the mapping that answers it. A reference off-chip DRAM access costs far more energy per event than arithmetic (figure 4), so reducing repeated external accesses improves efficiency. Deciding whether a given kernel is limited by compute throughput or by memory bandwidth, however, requires an analytical boundary. The roofline model supplies that boundary by comparing operational intensity against hardware performance limits, so that optimization effort targets the resource that actually binds.
