11.8 Compilers and Runtimes

The roofline gives each ResNet-50 layer a ceiling, and hardware mapping showed which schedules can approach it, but neither reaches the silicon by itself. Every layer needs a tiling, a stationary operand, a tensor layout, a precision for the activations it reads and writes, and a fusion boundary. The resulting plan must then run on a device whose input shapes, free memory, and clock rate change while it serves. Across a whole model these choices number in the thousands, which is why compilers and runtimes, not engineers, make them. Graph capture and dispatch overhead, which decide how a model reaches a compiler, belong to ML Frameworks, and the choice of a deployment runtime for a service belongs to Inference Runtime Selection. What remains here is lowering, the path from a captured graph to the accelerator’s units, and the runtime that executes the result. The decode floors this chapter quotes for GPT-2 XL assume that the step is launched as a captured graph (Graph capture and JIT compilation); executed one eager kernel at a time, launch overhead rather than memory bandwidth would set the floor.

A single convolution can be implemented with dozens of valid tiling strategies, kernel variants, and memory layouts, most of which perform poorly on a given target. Machine learning compilers navigate this space by translating high-level dataflow representations into target-specific executable code, making the mapping and dataflow decisions of the preceding sections automatically. Compiling ResNet-50 for GPU inference illustrates the core compiler stages:

  1. Graph optimization fuses repeated Conv2D-BatchNorm-ReLU patterns into single compound kernels, eliminating intermediate round-trips to HBM.
  2. Kernel selection chooses specialized Tensor Core implementations for compatible matrix multiplications, exploiting the high arithmetic intensity of dense convolutions.
  3. Memory planning determines activation lifetimes to safely overlap and reuse intermediate buffer allocations.
  4. Computation scheduling pipelines memory copies with execution across independent hardware queues to hide data transfer latencies.

↩︎ Graph compilation, kernel fusion, and framework dispatch overhead are established in Execution: From Graphs to Kernels.

On the reference H100, the modeled batch-one forward pass falls from 3.53 ms in an eager framework to 0.33 ms as a compiled FP16 engine, a 10.6× improvement without altering the model’s mathematical output. The arithmetic per image is unchanged. The gain comes from fusing the network’s 174 framework kernels into 56 and launching them as one graph instead of one Python dispatch at a time, which removes the fixed cost that dominates a single image. That answers the question the chapter opened with. The INT8 arithmetic for one image takes about 4 μs on the H100 (8 μs at FP16), so even the compiled pass spends almost all of its time on launch and overhead. Batch-one latency sits on the overhead floor rather than on either roofline ceiling, which is why halving the arithmetic barely moves it. The latencies are modeled rather than measured, and Inference Runtime Selection separates the same gap into the contribution of each runtime, but the mechanism is general. Graph rewrites, kernel selection, memory planning, and scheduling systematically apply kernel fusion (section 11.7.7) and memory-efficient tiling (section 11.7.5.1) to convert theoretical hardware FLOP/s into delivered throughput (Chen et al. 2018; NVIDIA 2024b).

11.8.1 ML compiler design

A conventional C++ compiler such as gcc or clang cannot collapse ResNet-50’s 174 framework dispatches into 56 fused kernels on its own, because by the time operators lower to scalar loops and pointer arithmetic, the high-level tensor algebra is gone. Machine learning compilers preserve that domain structure by operating on tensor graphs and operator libraries before lowering to machine code. Whereas general-purpose compilers optimize scalar control flow, vector instructions, register allocation, and cache locality, ML compiler stacks optimize graph topology, tensor memory layouts, shape specialization, accelerator kernel dispatch, and inter-device execution planning (Li et al. 2021). Table 15 contrasts the emphasis of these two compiler layers. The boundary is complementary rather than disjoint: an ML compiler stack lowers high-level tensor operations into intermediate representations that feed into an LLVM, GPU, or vendor-specific backend.

Li, Mingzhen, Yi Liu, Xiaoyan Liu, Qingxiao Sun, Xin You, Hailong Yang, Zhongzhi Luan, Lin Gan, Guangwen Yang, and Depei Qian. 2021. “The Deep Learning Compiler: A Comprehensive Survey.” IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems 32 (3): 708–27. https://doi.org/10.1109/tpds.2020.3030548.

The distinction in table 15 explains why compiler configuration dictates delivered performance even when the underlying neural network code remains unmodified. ML compilers manage the translation layer between high-level tensor operations and hardware execution units; when this mapping fails to expose reuse or efficient access, execution can be limited by memory traffic, latency, or insufficient parallel work.

11.8.2 ML compilation pipeline

Bridging those two compiler layers requires a staged ML compilation pipeline that progressively lowers a framework’s dataflow graph into executable code for CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, or custom ASICs (Chen et al. 2018; Google 2025; Lattner et al. 2020). A full production pipeline adds a fifth stage, code generation, to the four stages previewed on ResNet-50 (graph optimization, kernel selection, memory planning, and computation scheduling), emitting target-specific machine instructions, assembly, or interpreted bytecode. Across these five stages, the compiler applies the dataflow strategies developed in section 11.7.3: kernel fusion, memory tiling, and compute placement. Hardware acceleration delivers its theoretical throughput only when these compiler-driven transformations expose sufficient arithmetic intensity and align memory access with the hardware hierarchy.

Graph optimization

Machine learning frameworks represent models as high-level computation graphs, where nodes represent mathematical operators (such as convolutions, matrix multiplications, and activations) and directed edges represent tensor data dependencies. Executing each operator as a separate kernel can incur intermediate-buffer traffic and repeated launches. An edge denotes a dependency, not necessarily a new allocation or an off-chip transfer, and asynchronous dependencies need not synchronize the host. When intermediate materialization and dispatch dominate execution, graph transformations can remove substantial overhead.

Graph optimization transforms this computation graph into an efficient execution plan before hardware code generation (Chen et al. 2018; Jia et al. 2019). Working primarily at a target-independent intermediate representation (IR) level before lowering (section 11.8.2.5), graph passes apply four core transformations. Kernel fusion merges adjacent operations into a single compound kernel to eliminate off-chip memory round-trips and launch overheads. In convolutional networks, fusing Conv2D, batch normalization with frozen inference statistics, and ReLU keeps activations in local registers or shared SRAM throughout the sequence (section 11.7.7). In transformers, pattern matchers replace multi-operator self-attention subgraphs (score matrix multiplication, scaling, masking, softmax, and multiplication by the value matrix) with IO-aware attention kernels that keep active tiles and running reduction statistics in fast on-chip memory (Dao et al. 2022). Redundant computation elimination and constant folding remove work that need not happen at runtime at all. A typical case is folding frozen normalization parameters into the weights and biases of the preceding linear or convolutional layer (Compression-specific fusion). These passes also prune dead subgraphs and merge identical parallel paths through common subexpression elimination.

Jia, Zhihao, James Thomas, Todd Warszawski, Mingyu Gao, Matei Zaharia, and Alex Aiken. 2019. “Optimizing DNN Computation with Relaxed Graph Substitutions.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys).
Dao, T., D. Y. Fu, S. Ermon, A. Rudra, and C. Ré. 2022. “FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 16344–59. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1189.

The remaining two passes reduce data movement and live memory footprint without changing the operator set. Algebraic simplification and layout adjustments reorder mathematically equivalent operations to avoid runtime reshape traffic, for example by pushing transpositions through elementwise ops or canceling them against inverse permutations. Memory-aware node reordering evaluates topological sorts of the dependency graph. It schedules independent operations so intermediate activations are consumed and deallocated promptly before memory pressure forces spills to host DRAM. Production compilers execute these rewrites through pattern-matching rules, producing a coarse-grained execution graph aligned with the accelerator’s bandwidth constraints before binding each node to a concrete hardware routine.

Kernel selection

Kernel selection binds each node in the optimized graph to a concrete hardware implementation. Accelerators provide dozens of valid kernel implementations for a single tensor operation, each parameterized by tile dimensions, thread block configurations, memory staging patterns, and target precision. Choosing the optimal kernel determines whether the execution engine achieves high compute utilization or stalls on uncoalesced memory accesses and pipeline bubbles (Chen et al. 2018; Zheng et al. 2020).

In most production pipelines, compilers draw from vendor-optimized kernel libraries (NVIDIA’s cuDNN and cuBLAS for GPUs, Intel’s oneDNN for x86) rather than synthesizing kernels from scratch. These libraries encode microarchitectural details such as register file capacity, cache latency, and vector lane width, so the compiler can invoke pre-tuned implementations.

AI compilers trade compilation time against execution speed across three strategies when choosing among candidate kernels, with numerical precision constraining all three. Rule-based selection is the fastest at compile time. It relies on static heuristics over tensor shapes, alignment, data types, and target support to pick implementations such as a Tensor Core GEMM without benchmarking a large candidate set, at the risk of missing faster configurations on irregular shapes. Cost-model selection refines that choice without running hardware benchmarks by estimating kernel latency, register pressure, cache hit rates, and arithmetic intensity with analytical models that prune unpromising candidates (Lattner et al. 2020). When compilation budgets allow hardware measurement, profile-guided selection benchmarks candidates directly on the target device. Autotuners such as TVM’s AutoTVM and Ansor search over tile sizes, unrolling factors, and thread configurations to converge on the fastest implementation (Chen et al. 2018; Zheng et al. 2020), and TensorRT similarly times candidate tactics against the target batch sizes. Across all three strategies, precision-aware constraints govern which candidates are legal: inference can use lower-precision paths after quality validation, but selecting INT8 without appropriate range handling degrades accuracy, whereas selecting a wider path unnecessarily forgoes available throughput.

Lattner, Chris, Mehdi Amini, Uday Bondhugula, Albert Cohen, Andy Davis, Jacques Pienaar, River Riddle, Tatiana Shpeisman, Nicolas Vasilache, and Oleksandr Zinenko. 2020. “MLIR: Scaling Compiler Infrastructure for Domain Specific Computation.” 2021 IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO), 2–14. https://doi.org/10.1109/cgo51591.2021.9370308.

Memory planning

Memory planning assigns physical storage locations, buffer offsets, and tensor lifetimes across the accelerator’s memory hierarchy (Roesch et al. 2018; Chen et al. 2018). High-performance execution plans fail if memory management introduces uncoalesced memory transactions, bank conflicts, or unnecessary memory allocations that exhaust accelerator memory, so the compiler coordinates three core memory management mechanisms.

Google. 2025. XLA: Optimizing Compiler for Machine Learning.

Tensor layout optimization chooses the physical arrangement of tensor dimensions that each kernel needs for coalesced access and vectorization, such as channels-last NHWC for Tensor Core convolutions (section 11.7.6) (NVIDIA Corporation 2021; Google 2025). Compilers perform layout assignment globally across the graph to prevent back-to-back layout transformation kernels that consume memory bandwidth.

Liveness analysis and buffer reuse prevent out-of-memory errors by sharing physical memory across non-overlapping tensors. Deep neural networks generate dozens of intermediate activation tensors during forward propagation. Allocating a unique memory buffer for every tensor would quickly exceed the capacity of device memory (such as 16 to 80 GB on typical accelerator GPUs). The compiler analyzes the graph to compute the liveness interval of each tensor, from its generation to the completion of its last consumer. By modeling memory allocation as an interval graph coloring or 2D bin-packing problem, the compiler assigns multiple non-overlapping intermediate tensors to the same physical memory offsets (Roesch et al. 2018). This static reuse reduces peak device memory requirements to the working set size of concurrently active tensors, avoiding runtime allocation overhead and fragmentation.

Roesch, Jared, Steven Lyubomirsky, Logan Weber, Josh Pollock, Marisa Kirisame, Tianqi Chen, and Zachary Tatlock. 2018. “Relay: A New IR for Machine Learning Frameworks.” Proceedings of the 2nd ACM SIGPLAN International Workshop on Machine Learning and Programming Languages, 58–68. https://doi.org/10.1145/3211346.3211348.

Memory hierarchy placement optimizes the staging of data between external memory (HBM or GDDR) and on-chip scratchpad memories (SRAM or shared memory). External memory bandwidth is a scarce resource; moving intermediate tiles back and forth across the memory bus creates memory-bound stalls. Compilers synthesize tiling parameters that guarantee intermediate blocks remain resident in on-chip SRAM until all local compute operations complete, minimizing round-trip traffic across the memory bus. With memory layouts fixed and buffer addresses assigned, the compiler schedules operation execution across hardware compute resources.

Computation scheduling

Computation scheduling determines the execution timeline and hardware resource binding for operations in the compiled graph (Zheng et al. 2020). Modern accelerators feature deep hardware pipelines, multiple independent compute engines, and dedicated DMA copy engines. Effective scheduling coordinates these resources across three distinct architectural dimensions to maximize hardware occupancy, preserve data dependencies, and prevent pipeline stalls (Chen et al. 2018).

Norrie, Thomas, Nishant Patil, Doe Hyun Yoon, George Kurian, Sheng Li, James Laudon, Cliff Young, Norman Jouppi, and David Patterson. 2021. “The Design Process for Google’s Training Chips: TPUv2 and TPUv3.” IEEE Micro 41 (2): 56–63. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2021.3058217.

Task partitioning maps computational subgraphs onto the target’s physical execution units. On GPUs, computations are partitioned into grids of thread blocks dispatched across Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs). On TPUs, matrix multiplications are partitioned into tile sequences matched to the physical dimensions of systolic arrays (e.g., \(128 \times 128\) or \(256 \times 256\) processing elements) (Norrie et al. 2021). On CPUs, tasks are split into thread pools matching physical cores and vectorized to fill SIMD registers.

Execution ordering resolves dependencies while minimizing live memory pressure. Operations that depend on prior results must wait for producer kernels to complete, but independent branches (such as multi-head attention projections or parallel residual paths) can execute concurrently or interleave to maintain uniform compute utilization. Compilers analyze the dependency graph to schedule operations in an order that keeps compute pipelines full while keeping activation lifetimes short, preventing buffer bloat.

Asynchronous overlap hides memory latency by executing data transfers concurrently with compute kernels. Accelerators feature dedicated DMA engines that operate independently of arithmetic pipelines. Compilers exploit this architectural separation by scheduling memory transfers (such as host-to-device weights or inter-accelerator halo exchanges) in separate hardware queues or CUDA streams, overlapping transfer latency behind long-running compute operations (Chen et al. 2018; NVIDIA 2024b). When compute and transfer overlap completely, data movement costs are hidden behind arithmetic execution. Poor scheduling instead introduces execution bubbles where arithmetic units sit idle waiting for kernel dispatches or serialized data copies, so synchronizing kernels via explicit compiler-generated events and stream schedules ensures the hardware sustains continuous execution without CPU driver intervention (NVIDIA 2024b; Zheng et al. 2020).

Chen, Tianqi, Thierry Moreau, Ziheng Jiang, Lianmin Zheng, Eddie Q. Yan, Haichen Shen, Meghan Cowan, et al. 2018. “TVM: An Automated End-to-End Optimizing Compiler for Deep Learning.” Proceedings of the 13th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI ’18), 578–94.
NVIDIA. 2024b. NVIDIA TensorRT: Programmable Inference Accelerator.
Zheng, Lianmin, Chengfan Jia, Minmin Sun, Zhao Wu, Cody Hao Yu, Ameer Haj-Ali, Yida Wang, et al. 2020. “Ansor: Generating High-Performance Tensor Programs for Deep Learning.” Proceedings of the 14th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI), 863–79.

Code generation

With scheduling complete, the final compilation stage translates the scheduled execution plan into target-specific machine instructions. Code generation applies traditional backend compiler passes (instruction selection, register allocation, instruction scheduling, and peephole optimization) tailored to accelerator architectures.

Instruction selection for ML targets must emit instructions that directly engage specialized matrix ISA extensions. On NVIDIA GPUs, code generators emit PTX instructions such as mma.sync.aligned to invoke Tensor Cores directly, as shown in listing 13. On Intel CPUs with Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX), the backend targets tile-multiply instructions operating on 2D register tiles. On Arm architectures with the Scalable Matrix Extension (SME), the target is outer-product accumulation across scalable vector tiles. A backend that emits generic floating-point vector instructions instead of these matrix extensions leaves the primary compute engines idle, reducing effective throughput by an order of magnitude. For CPUs and GPUs, compilers emit machine code or optimized assembly; for TPUs, field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs),27 and proprietary NPUs, the output is often an optimized bytecode or binary execution package executed by a specialized hardware runtime.

27 Field-programmable gate array: “Field-programmable” means the logic fabric is configurable after manufacturing, contrasting with fixed-function ASICs. FPGAs can improve performance for latency-sensitive data center services by implementing custom pipelines matched to a particular workload (Putnam et al. 2014). This reconfigurability makes FPGAs attractive for rapidly evolving ML architectures where committing to an ASIC risks obsolescence, but the requirement for hardware description languages (Verilog/VHDL) and compilation times measured in hours creates a productivity barrier that limits adoption to deployments where the efficiency benefit justifies the engineering cost.

Putnam, Andrew, Adrian M. Caulfield, Eric S. Chung, Derek Chiou, Kypros Constantinides, John Demme, Hadi Esmaeilzadeh, et al. 2014. “A Reconfigurable Fabric for Accelerating Large-Scale Datacenter Services.” ACM SIGARCH Computer Architecture News 42 (3): 13–24. https://doi.org/10.1145/2678373.2665678.

11.8.3 Runtime support

A compiler transforms a high-level model into an execution plan tailored to target hardware, but that plan embeds static assumptions about runtime conditions: tensor shapes, workspace allocation limits, device capabilities, and execution concurrency. Ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation optimizes graph structures, fusion boundaries, and memory layouts for fixed shapes and known hardware configurations. While just-in-time (JIT) compilation can compile specialized variants dynamically as new shapes arrive, each compiled kernel still executes a fixed execution plan. Production serving breaks those assumptions: request arrival rates fluctuate, batch sizes vary, several inference workloads compete for shared accelerator memory, and thermal throttling can pull clock frequencies below their rated values. Request batching and admission control belong to the serving layer (Model Serving); the concern here is how the accelerator runtime dispatches compiled execution plans once a batch reaches the hardware.

An AI runtime bridges static graph compilation and the dynamic realities of accelerator execution. Compilers optimize and lower computational graphs under fixed structural assumptions, but production systems encounter variable batch sizes, fluctuating sequence lengths, and constrained memory budgets. The runtime executes compiled engines while managing input-dependent tensor shapes, device-memory buffers and workspace, asynchronous hardware streams, and precompiled execution profiles. In production inference stacks such as NVIDIA TensorRT, the offline builder optimizes the network and benchmarks candidate tactics to construct an execution engine, while the runtime engine binds input buffers, selects valid optimization profiles, and dispatches kernels to the accelerator (NVIDIA Corporation 2026a, 2026b).

NVIDIA Corporation. 2026a. How TensorRT Works.
NVIDIA Corporation. 2026b. Working with Dynamic Shapes.
Huang, Y., Y. Cheng, A. Bapna, O. Firat, D. Chen, M. X. Chen, H. Lee, et al. 2019. “GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks Using Pipeline Parallelism.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 32: 103–12.
Mirhoseini, Azalia, Hieu Pham, Quoc V. Le, Benoit Steiner, Rasmus Larsen, Yuefeng Zhou, Naveen Kumar, Mohammad Norouzi, Samy Bengio, and Jeff Dean. 2017. “Device Placement Optimization with Reinforcement Learning.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 70: 2430–39.

This execution lifecycle spans three core responsibilities. First, the runtime selects and dispatches precompiled kernel variants matched to runtime tensor dimensions and hardware capabilities. Second, it manages device memory through arena allocators and static buffer reuse, reducing repeated allocation and associated host-device synchronization overhead. Third, in distributed environments, framework runtimes coordinate cross-device execution boundaries, as demonstrated in pipeline-parallel frameworks such as GPipe (Huang et al. 2019) and automated device-placement systems (Mirhoseini et al. 2017). While serving schedulers oversee request batching and admission control across clusters, the accelerator runtime governs local execution on the device.

ML runtime architecture

General-purpose runtimes manage threads, preemptive tasks, heap allocations, and asynchronous I/O across arbitrary control-flow paths. In contrast, an AI runtime operates over dataflow graphs composed of multidimensional tensors, pre-scheduled kernel grids, device memory arenas, and hardware command queues, as contrasted in table 16.

Tensor memory management represents a primary architectural divergence. In traditional systems, general-purpose allocators manage variable-sized heap objects using runtime metadata. Traditional device allocation calls such as cudaMalloc can introduce costly driver work and synchronization. AI runtimes reduce repeated allocation overhead by combining lifetime analysis with pooled or arena allocation. For fixed-shape graphs, the compiler computes static memory offsets, mapping non-overlapping intermediate tensors to shared physical buffers. For variable-shape tensors, the runtime can carve device-memory buffers from preallocated pools, avoiding repeated driver allocation calls within the reserved capacity.

Production environments introduce physical constraints that differ from offline benchmarks. For example, an NVIDIA A100 SXM accelerator operates with a maximum TDP of 400 W, whereas the A100 PCIe variant is constrained to a 300 W TDP envelope. Because sustained clock frequencies scale with available power and thermal dissipation, a compiled kernel tuned for an SXM module may experience thermal throttling or fail to meet latency bounds on a PCIe card. The runtime cannot re-synthesize loop structures or change thread-block dimensions dynamically in response to thermal constraints; it must execute within precompiled profiles while the serving system handles request batching and admission control.

Dynamic kernel execution

While static compilation generates high-performance machine code for fixed shapes, production inference requires executing requests with dynamic dimensions. In language models, input sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) and batch size \(\BatchSize\) vary across requests. Recompiling an execution plan for each unexpected shape can violate a request deadline: exploring loop unrolling, shared-memory tiling, and register allocation requires seconds or minutes, while serving deadlines operate on millisecond timescales.

↪ How serving runtimes form batches of varying size under latency deadlines is developed in Static vs. dynamic batching.

Profile-based inference stacks address this mismatch with precompiled shape ranges. The engine is built for a declared range of each dynamic dimension (the minimum, typical, and maximum shapes), with device-memory workspace reserved for that range. A request inside the range binds its tensors to preallocated buffers and launches precompiled kernels without compilation overhead. A request outside it must be padded, split, or routed to a slower general-purpose kernel, because the runtime cannot synthesize new tiling strategies on the fly. TensorRT’s optimization profiles are the common example, and choosing and configuring such a runtime for a service is developed in Inference Runtime Selection.

Variable requests also keep the host link busy, and the runtime hides those transfers with the asynchronous streams and double buffering of section 11.5.4.2, copying batch \(\BatchIndex{+}1\) while batch \(\BatchIndex\) executes. The overlap holds only while compute duration exceeds transfer duration.

Runtime kernel selection

An operation may have multiple kernel implementations, termed tactics in TensorRT. The builder selects tactics while constructing an engine; other stacks may retain variants for runtime dispatch. The available choice depends on tensor dimensions, the compiled plan, and permitted device-memory workspace.

Operational batch size changes the available reuse and parallelism. At \(\BatchSize=1\) in weight-streaming autoregressive decoding, GEMV kernels often target memory throughput. Larger prompt-processing batches can favor GEMM kernels using Tensor Core paths, register tiles, and shared memory. The transition depends on dimensions, precision, traffic, and hardware balance; no fixed batch threshold establishes compute-bound execution.

Device-memory workspace availability further constrains tactic selection. In a standard output-tiled GEMM, each thread block computes one \((\GemmRowDimension, \GemmColumnDimension)\) output tile and loops sequentially over the entire inner reduction dimension \(\GemmInnerDimension\), accumulating partial sums in on-chip registers before writing the final output tile once. When the output matrix is small but the reduction dimension \(\GemmInnerDimension\) is long, the output grid spawns too few thread blocks to occupy every streaming multiprocessor. A split-\(\GemmInnerDimension\) tactic exposes extra parallelism by partitioning the \(\GemmInnerDimension\) reduction loop across multiple thread blocks running on different multiprocessors. Because separate multiprocessors do not share registers or local scratchpad memory, each split-\(\GemmInnerDimension\) block must write its partial tile sum to a temporary buffer in global device memory so a subsequent reduction step can sum the slices into the final result. A runtime execution plan built under a tight workspace memory limit may therefore disallow split-\(\GemmInnerDimension\) tactics and accept lower multiprocessor occupancy instead.

Runtime selection remains strictly bounded by the numerical formats established during compilation. In mixed-precision training and inference systems such as Megatron-LM, executing matrix multiplications in FP16 or BF16 on Tensor Cores with FP32 accumulation is a numerical requirement of the chosen recipe, validated prior to deployment (Shoeybi et al. 2019). The runtime does not monitor loss values or dynamically alter precision; it only chooses among the validated tactics that implement the specified numerical precision.

Shoeybi, Mohammad, Mostofa Patwary, Raul Puri, Patrick LeGresley, Jared Casper, and Bryan Catanzaro. 2019. “Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1909.08053.

Kernel scheduling and utilization

Kernel dispatch represents the final stage of runtime execution, coordinating host-side task queues with device-side execution. The software runtime manages host-side command queues (such as CUDA streams or TPU command rings) and records hardware events or semaphores to enforce dataflow dependencies asynchronously. When independent operations (such as parallel multi-head attention projections) have no mutual data dependencies, the runtime dispatches them onto separate streams to enable concurrent execution on the accelerator. Once submitted to the device queue, however, execution control transfers entirely to hardware schedulers. On a GPU, the hardware warp scheduler and work distribution engine assign thread blocks to SMs based on register file availability, shared memory capacity, and maximum warp occupancy. The software runtime cannot schedule individual threads or dictate L1/L2 cache replacement policies. Similarly, TPU runtimes submit macro-instructions to on-chip command queues, while hardware sequencers feed systolic matrix units and vector units (Jouppi et al. 2017).

A low achieved rate alone cannot distinguish runtime gaps from a memory bottleneck. Consider three supplied illustrative profiles of low-intensity kernels, not measurements from a particular device. In the first, the timeline shows continuous kernel execution and HBM traffic close to the sustainable bandwidth ceiling. Reducing transferred bytes or increasing reuse addresses that observed limit. In the second, kernels remain active but dependent loads produce long stalls while HBM traffic stays well below its ceiling. More bandwidth alone need not help: independent requests or a different access schedule must expose enough concurrency to hide the latency. In the third, short kernels alternate with device-idle gaps while the host submits work. Reducing dispatch and synchronization overhead addresses those gaps; changing the arithmetic instruction rate does not.

The discriminating evidence is the timeline together with traffic and stall observations. If added independent requests raise bandwidth and shorten load stalls, they support the latency hypothesis; if bandwidth is already sustained near its ceiling, traffic reduction is the more direct lever. The roofline bounds the resource opportunity, while the profile identifies which mechanism leaves the kernel below it. Even with aggressive kernel fusion, optimal tactic selection, and zero-allocation memory reuse, the execution capacity of a single accelerator is physically bounded by its silicon area, thermal dissipation limit, and high-bandwidth memory capacity. Scaling beyond these physical boundaries therefore requires distributing computation across multiple accelerators.

    3. To predict the number of training epochs required for a neural network to converge

11.9 Beyond One Accelerator

A single accelerator holds the chapter’s ResNet-50 workload and GPT-2 XL decoding comfortably in on-package memory, but larger workloads outgrow one device either because their arithmetic would take too long on it or because their weights and runtime state do not fit in its HBM. Multi-chip scaling still depends on an efficient per-device dataflow, since each accelerator must feed its own execution units, but communication adds further boundaries to the memory hierarchy. Moving data through on-chip storage, HBM, an intra-node link, and a network fabric generally increases latency and energy at each step, so scaling is not merely a question of adding chips.

Each step outward moves the communication boundary and changes the dominant trade-off. Inside the package, chiplet-based architectures partition a large design into smaller dies joined at relatively low latency, bypassing the manufacturing limits of a monolithic chip. Wafer-scale integration takes the opposite approach and keeps more computation on one device. At the node, a multi-accelerator server joins several chips, each with its own memory, through board- or server-level interconnects such as NVLink. A workload then splits through data parallelism (each accelerator processes different batches) or model parallelism (different accelerators hold different layers, or individual matrix multiplications are sliced across devices). When a model’s weights and runtime state exceed one device’s HBM, that split becomes a placement requirement rather than a speed choice. How training uses the accelerators of one machine, including how they synchronize gradients, is developed in Single-node multi-GPU training. Within a server, the engineering test compares the computation or device-memory capacity that partitioning saves with the communication it exposes, accounting for overlap and the actual directional link bandwidth.

Beyond the node, the network interface card links each machine to the others over Ethernet or InfiniBand. It is the narrowest, highest-latency step of the bandwidth taper measured in section 11.5.4.1, and traffic that must cross it leaves single-node reasoning behind. Work that spans several machines lies beyond this book’s one-machine scope. Scaling out across identical data-center accelerators is one way a system combines multiple engines; at the opposite end of the power spectrum, mobile and embedded systems integrate several different engines onto a single silicon die.

11.10 Heterogeneous SoC Design

Edge, mobile, and automotive deployments operate under strict physical constraints: sealed enclosures without active fans limit thermal dissipation to a few watts, while battery capacity caps total energy consumption. To deliver machine learning capabilities within these boundaries, heterogeneous system-on-chip (SoC) architectures integrate general-purpose CPU cores, GPU shader arrays, digital signal processors (DSPs), and specialized neural processing units (NPUs) onto a single silicon die sharing a unified memory subsystem. The workload mapping problem introduced for discrete accelerators persists, but it expands to include hardware operator coverage, cross-engine transfer overheads, real-time deadlines, and dynamic thermal throttling. Two of the book’s lighthouses take over from ResNet-50 here. MobileNetV2, compute-bound in its efficient regime and built for phone cameras, runs its convolutions on a phone’s NPU within a few watts. KWS, the power-bound lighthouse, listens continuously on a DSP or microcontroller within milliwatts. Both run on silicon that shares one memory system among every engine on the chip.

11.10.1 Mobile SoC architecture evolution

That single-die integration evolved as mobile workloads outgrew what a CPU and graphics pipeline could sustain within a battery budget. Mobile system-on-chip architectures implement heterogeneous computing by connecting each specialized block, namely CPU clusters, wide SIMD GPU shaders, fixed-point DSPs, and dedicated neural processing units (NPUs), over an on-chip network to shared low-power DRAM (LPDDR) so sensory and perceptual tasks can run on the engine best aligned with their arithmetic structure. Continuous audio feature extraction and keyword spotting run on low-power DSPs, dense convolution and matrix-multiplication layers execute on systolic or tensor-array NPUs, parallel graphics and image postprocessing map to GPUs, and sequential control flow runs on the CPU. Meeting real-time frame deadlines without triggering aggressive thermal throttling requires scheduling execution across these engines while respecting their differing power profiles.

Example 11.5: Heterogeneous microcontrollers
Scenario: An embedded smart doorbell must run periodic person detection within a tight memory, energy, and latency budget.

Diagnosis: On a supported deployment, a general-purpose Cortex-M path misses the measured energy or latency target. A micro-NPU such as Arm Ethos-U can offload compatible convolution operators, while the CPU retains control flow and unsupported operations.

Systems lesson: Micro-NPU specialization can improve the energy and latency of supported operators, but feasibility must be measured for the whole pipeline, including fallbacks and sensor processing.

Modern mobile SoCs use unified memory architectures where all processing units share a common physical address space in LPDDR. Unlike discrete accelerator architectures that incur explicit PCIe transfer latencies, unified memory allows zero-copy buffer passing between the image signal processor (ISP), CPU, GPU, and NPU. Sharing physical DRAM does not guarantee zero software overhead, however. Non-coherent engines need explicit cache maintenance (section 11.10.4), and specialized NPUs often require hardware-specific tensor layouts (such as channels-last (NHWC) with 16- or 32-byte channel alignment to feed vector register lanes), forcing memory-bound transpositions when interfacing with CPU layers structured in channels-first (NCHW) formats.

SoC architects customize these compute blocks according to domain-specific physical constraints. High-end smartphone SoCs emphasize peak burst performance and low idle leakage for interactive tasks such as real-time computational photography and on-device text generation. In contrast, embedded and automotive SoCs prioritize deterministic memory access, hardware fault detection, and bounded worst-case latency to satisfy real-time control constraints.

11.10.2 Strategies for dynamic workload distribution

Consider a real-time object detection pipeline executing on a mobile SoC with an integrated CPU, GPU, and NPU. The pipeline comprises three consecutive stages: a MobileNetV2 backbone for feature extraction, nonmaximum suppression (NMS) for postprocessing candidate bounding boxes, and a display overlay to render final detections onto a camera feed. Partitioning neural network workloads across those heterogeneous cores requires matching the arithmetic intensity and memory regularity of each stage to the microarchitecture built for it. The convolutional backbone has regular, deterministic memory access and dense arithmetic suited to the NPU’s fixed-function tensor engine, even though depthwise separable layers have lower arithmetic intensity than standard convolutions. NMS, by contrast, relies on score-based sorting and conditional intersection-over-union loops evaluated across variable-length candidate lists. This irregular, branch-heavy control flow maps poorly to an NPU’s spatial array but executes efficiently on out-of-order CPU cores with branch prediction and hardware caching. Finally, the display overlay requires per-pixel rasterization and alpha blending across a high-resolution frame (an embarrassingly parallel, memory-bandwidth-bound task that maps directly to the GPU’s rasterizers and texture units). Splitting the pipeline across the three engines, with the NPU for feature extraction, the CPU for NMS, and the GPU for display compositing, is a candidate mapping. Its compute savings must exceed transfer, layout, and synchronization costs before it improves end-to-end latency or energy over a single-engine implementation.

This pipeline partitioning reflects the broader relationship between algorithmic structures and machine architectures. Regular matrix contractions and convolutions map cleanly to systolic or vectorized NPU datapaths, whereas data-dependent control flow maps to CPU execution resources. Transformer attention layers span both paradigms: the projection GEMMs (\(\AttentionQueryMatrix, \AttentionKeyMatrix, \AttentionValuesMatrix, \AttentionOutputMatrix\)) and attention score contractions (\(\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T\), and the product of the attention weights with \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\)) execute efficiently on NPU matrix units. Intermediate softmax reductions, causal masking, and layer normalizations, however, involve elementwise operations. If the NPU runtime cannot fuse these elementwise operations into on-chip SRAM scratchpads, intermediate tensors must spill to LPDDR, eroding the accelerator’s throughput advantage.

Optimal processor assignment is dynamic rather than static. As device thermal conditions deteriorate or battery reserves drop, the runtime must adapt its scheduling policy. However, migrating an executing model across processor backends carries non-trivial overhead: weights must be re-bound in memory, intermediate buffers may require layout reformatting, and device drivers incur kernel dispatch latency. If the overhead of synchronizing state across processors exceeds the compute savings of offloading, retaining execution on a single suboptimal engine can yield lower total latency and energy than continuous cross-engine migration.

Shared memory subsystems introduce cross-engine interference during simultaneous execution. Because the CPU, GPU, NPU, camera ISP, and display engine share a single LPDDR memory bus, the SoC memory controller enforces Quality of Service (QoS) priorities to satisfy real-time hardware deadlines. The display engine and camera ISP must receive guaranteed memory bandwidth and bounded latency to prevent display flicker and sensor FIFO overflow; the memory controller consequently prioritizes display and camera transactions over NPU and GPU traffic. During memory-intensive phases (such as autoregressive language model decoding where model weights must be read from DRAM for every generated token) high-priority ISP or display traffic reduces effective NPU memory bandwidth, increasing token generation latency.

Automotive computing platforms expose a stricter form of the same interference. A perception pipeline with a hard deadline may share the SoC and memory system with a cabin assistant or infotainment model. If the convenience workload streams weights from DRAM without a bandwidth limit, it can delay the perception pipeline even when the two use different compute engines. Such deployments require resource isolation and validation under concurrent load; average inference throughput alone cannot establish deadline compliance. The hardware lesson is the interference boundary: assigning work to separate engines does not isolate workloads that still share memory bandwidth.

11.10.3 Power and thermal management

Fanless mobile devices operate within strict continuous power budgets and thermal envelopes, typically dissipating no more than 3 to 5 watts sustained across the entire chassis before touch temperatures exceed safety thresholds. Although transient bursts can draw 10 to 15 watts, continuous inference rapidly saturates the thermal capacitance of the device, heating the silicon junction and requiring active power management across the SoC.

Heterogeneous SoCs manage power across distinct silicon partitions using dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), which exploits the cubic dependence of dynamic power on frequency behind the power wall (equation 2.2). Total power in complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) digital circuits is the sum of dynamic switching power and static leakage power: \[\TotalChipPower= \DynamicPower+ \LeakagePower= \SwitchingActivityFactor \SwitchedCapacitance \SupplyVoltage^2 \ClockFrequency+ \LeakageCurrent \SupplyVoltage\] where \(\SwitchingActivityFactor\) is the gate switching activity factor, \(\SwitchedCapacitance\) is physical load capacitance, \(\SupplyVoltage\) is supply voltage, \(\ClockFrequency\) is clock frequency, and \(\LeakageCurrent\) is temperature-dependent leakage current. Over an operating range where increasing clock frequency \(\ClockFrequency\) requires supply voltage \(\SupplyVoltage\) to rise approximately proportionally, fixed activity and capacitance give the cubic approximation for dynamic power dissipation: \[\DynamicPower\propto \ClockFrequency^3\] Under that approximation, doubling clock frequency can incur an eightfold penalty in dynamic power (Le Sueur and Heiser 2010). The same relation run in reverse is what DVFS exploits: dropping the clock lets the core voltage fall, and dynamic power falls faster than throughput. The cubic penalty also explains why ML accelerators favor large parallel arrays of simple execution units clocked at moderate frequencies over narrow pipelines clocked at extreme frequencies.

Le Sueur, Etienne, and Gernot Heiser. 2010. “Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling: The Laws of Diminishing Returns.” Proceedings of the 2010 International Conference on Power Aware Computing and Systems, 1–8.

On a heterogeneous SoC, CPU clusters, GPU shader cores, and NPU engines occupy separate power and voltage domains. Increasing the voltage and frequency of the NPU to meet a tight latency deadline consumes electrical current and thermal headroom that would otherwise be available to the CPU or GPU. System power governors continuously adjust these operating points based on workload queues, temperature sensor readings, and frame deadline targets.

When sustained computation exceeds the chassis dissipation rate, the platform initiates thermal throttling. Because specialized NPUs achieve higher energy efficiency (TOPS/W) for tensor math than general-purpose cores, offloading matrix workloads to a CPU or GPU during a thermal event often increases total energy dissipation, exacerbating thermal accumulation. Instead, runtimes manage thermal limits by capping clock frequencies, reducing inference duty cycles (such as throttling a perception model from 30 frames per second to 15 frames per second), or dynamically switching to a smaller, pruned model checkpoint. Task migration is applied selectively to move non-tensor preprocessing away from localized silicon hot spots on the die. Battery state further shapes runtime scheduling. When battery charge drops below critical thresholds or the device enters a low-power mode, the system scheduler trades inferencing fidelity for battery life. It does so by selecting prevalidated lower-precision or sparse model variants, or by batching asynchronous inference requests to maximize the time cores spend in deep low-power sleep states.

11.10.4 Software stack challenges

When a model deployed on an SoC contains even a single operator unsupported by the NPU delegate (such as a custom activation, dynamic tensor shape, or non-standard reduction), the inference runtime must split the computation graph into subgraphs and insert fallback paths to the CPU or GPU. Each boundary crossing requires synchronizing execution and translating data representations, transforming a single algorithmic graph into a fragmented sequence of hardware dispatches. Standard programming models like OpenCL and Vulkan provide portable low-level execution abstractions across compute devices, but they do not eliminate this delegation overhead or the need for microarchitecture-specific kernel tuning.

Shared memory subsystems require explicit cache and memory management across non-coherent execution domains. While CPUs maintain cache coherence across their own cores via hardware snooping protocols, mobile NPUs and DSPs frequently interface with system memory as non-coherent DMA bus masters. When the CPU writes input tensors to cached DRAM and hands control to an NPU, software must explicitly flush the CPU’s dirty cache lines to DRAM before NPU execution begins. Similarly, upon NPU completion, the CPU must invalidate its own cache lines over the destination memory range to prevent reading stale cached data. If unsupported operators cause an inference graph to ping-pong repeatedly between CPU and NPU, the latency of cache maintenance and intermediate DRAM round-trips can exceed the execution time of the operators themselves.

Runtimes navigate this scheduling complexity using ahead-of-time compilation, empirical profile databases, and dynamic dispatch heuristics. Device telemetry (monitoring frame completion times, core temperatures, and battery drain) informs runtime decisions to throttle clock frequencies or swap execution delegates. However, dynamic adaptation cannot replace deterministic graph lowering for latency-sensitive applications; deployment requires validating the compiled, lowered partition on physical target silicon under worst-case thermal and memory contention.

On an SoC, speed comes from keeping work and data on the right engine, not from how many engines the chip has. In the D·A·M taxonomy, an SoC represents a composite Machine layer whose components have different memory hierarchies, arithmetic strengths, and thermal envelopes. The iron law’s data term and the energy-movement principle (7) together make data movement the governor of both runtime and energy. When software coordination fails to maintain tensor locality or induces frequent cross-engine fallbacks, energy dissipation is dominated by interconnect and DRAM traffic rather than arithmetic. Maximizing performance on heterogeneous SoCs requires minimizing data movement across domain boundaries while matching each algorithmic operation to the specialized datapath architected to accelerate it. From the microcontroller that runs keyword spotting to the data-center accelerator that serves GPT-2 XL, that matching ends in a choice of machine, which the next section makes explicit.

    1. The high-performance ‘big’ CPU core running single-threaded FP32 instructions
    2. The out-of-order system memory controller
    3. The dedicated Neural Processing Unit (NPU) optimized for quantized INT8 tensor operations

11.11 Choosing an Accelerator

Every section of this chapter ends in the same question asked at a different level: which machine should run a given workload. The question cannot be answered from a datasheet, because the resource that binds belongs to the workload on a particular machine rather than to the machine alone. The book’s five lighthouses make the point on a single reference machine. Their bytes and operations differ by orders of magnitude, and each one exhausts a different resource of an H100 first (table 17).

The table turns the chapter’s diagnosis into a selection rule. ResNet-50 rewards arithmetic throughput on a supported INT8 path, GPT-2 XL decode rewards memory bandwidth, DLRM rewards memory capacity, and MobileNetV2 and KWS reward energy per inference on chips that never see a data center. The rest of the section applies that rule at three levels: the configurations accelerator families adopt for their target deployments, the cost of delivered throughput, and the energy each request consumes.

11.11.1 Processor configurations across deployment targets

Across data-center, server-CPU, and mobile targets, architects assemble SIMD lanes, Tensor Cores, and systolic arrays into markedly different full-chip organizations depending on which resource binds first. Training-optimized accelerators such as the NVIDIA A100 pack 108 Streaming Multiprocessors with wide SIMD units and FP16 Tensor Cores because training throughput scales with aggregate multiply-accumulate capacity across general kernels (NVIDIA Corporation 2020a). Google’s TPU v4, by contrast, concentrates each chip into two cores built around large \(128{\times}128\) BF16 systolic arrays, trading per-thread flexibility for area and energy efficiency on dense matrix multiplications (Jouppi et al. 2023). Inference and edge targets shift the balance again. Intel’s Sapphire Rapids dedicates Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) tile engines to INT8 and BF16 because server inference models tolerate reduced precision (Intel Corporation 2021a), while mobile neural engines shrink those matrix datapaths into low-power SoC blocks that prioritize energy per operation over peak throughput. Table 18 compares these architectural configurations.

Jouppi, Norm, George Kurian, Sheng Li, Peter Ma, Rahul Nagarajan, Lifeng Nai, Nishant Patil, et al. 2023. “TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings.” Proceedings of the 50th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3579371.3589350.
Intel Corporation. 2021a. “Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel AMX).” Intel Architecture Instruction Set Extensions Programming Reference.

The pattern across these configurations reveals a consistent engineering principle: each design sacrifices generality to optimize for its target workload’s dominant operation and precision. Training chips invest silicon in wide floating-point datapaths; inference chips trade precision for throughput; mobile chips trade throughput for energy efficiency. No single design dominates across all workloads, which is precisely why hardware selection depends on workload analysis rather than headline specifications.

11.11.2 Cost-performance analysis

Consider an engineering team choosing between deploying a larger cluster of older accelerators or a smaller cluster of newer units. Architectural specifications define computational potential, but procurement decisions require cost-performance analysis grounded in delivered throughput rather than datasheet peaks. Because memory access costs dominate computation (section 11.2.3), accelerators achieve only a fraction of their advertised FLOP/s on memory-bound kernels while sustaining high utilization on dense matrix multiplications that amortize each fetch across many operations.

Peak FLOP/s figures therefore mislead whenever dominant kernels are memory-bandwidth or communication bound. In a large model pipeline, dense feed-forward and attention projection layers may remain compute bound, whereas embedding lookups, layer normalization, residual additions, and small-batch autoregressive decoding often have low arithmetic intensity. Their measured bottlenecks can include memory bandwidth, dependent access latency, reductions, and launch overhead; the operator name alone does not identify the limiting resource. The decisive metric is delivered workload throughput per dollar under realistic cluster utilization, memory capacity constraints, available memory bandwidth, and scale-out interconnect efficiency.

These architectural and economic constraints explain the rapid industry adoption of newer accelerators despite substantial increases in nominal unit price. For bandwidth-bound workloads, generational improvements in memory bandwidth and compiler code generation dominate end-to-end execution time. Cloud deployments introduce additional trade-offs: hourly rental rates, dynamic instance utilization, and infrastructure overhead continuously shift the economic break-even point between purchasing on-premises hardware and leasing cloud capacity.

Price-per-peak worksheets for named products age quickly. List prices vary with vendor, region, contract terms, and procurement volume, and each product’s headline peak uses a different precision, so the ratio of price to peak is meaningful for one device but not as a comparison across devices. A dated worksheet for several accelerator generations is kept with the other specifications in System Assumptions. The durable rule is the one the lighthouse table states: divide cost by the throughput the workload delivers on its binding resource, not by the advertised peak.

No worksheet reduces accelerator selection to a single headline specification. A bandwidth-bound kernel benefits more from the H100’s 3,350 GB/s memory subsystem than from an incremental gain in peak arithmetic, whereas a compute-bound GEMM shows the opposite sensitivity. Device memory capacity dictates whether working sets fit on-chip without spilling or partitioning, while compiler and driver maturity determines whether the application can actually reach the advertised datapath.

11.11.3 Energy per request

At fleet scale, energy per useful inference becomes an important hardware-selection criterion. Operational emissions depend on workload throughput, measured system power, utilization, cooling overhead, and the electricity mix; embodied emissions add another lifecycle cost. Peak performance per watt is therefore a screening metric, not a substitute for end-to-end energy per request. The following scenario shows how useful throughput and a common power boundary determine the fleet needed for the same inference service.

Napkin Math 11.11: An illustrative operational-energy comparison
Problem: An inference service must complete 1 billion requests per day. Which of two hypothetical server platforms uses less operational energy for that service?

Supplied observations: For the same model, input distribution, accuracy, and latency target, a CPU server sustains 100 requests/s, and an NPU-equipped server sustains 1,000 requests/s. Their whole-server wall powers are 100 W and 200 W, respectively, including hosts and attached accelerators. These are hypothetical observations for this exercise, not product benchmarks. Assume requests arrive steadily through the day. Both fleets operate at no more than 80 percent of the supplied throughput to reserve capacity for arrival-rate variation. Assume the listed wall power throughout the 24 h day, including spare capacity. Facility cooling and embodied emissions are outside this operational boundary.

Calculation:

  1. Size the fleets from useful work. Multiplying useful throughput by the operating fraction and the day length gives 6,912,000 requests per CPU server per day and 69,120,000 per NPU-equipped server. Divide the daily target by each capacity and round up to whole servers. The service requires 145 CPU servers or 15 NPU-equipped servers.
  2. Account for the provisioned fleet. Server count multiplied by wall power and day length yields 348 kWh per day for CPUs and 72 kWh for NPUs. Dividing each fleet’s energy by the same completed-request target gives 1.2528 J per request and 0.2592 J per request. These values include capacity headroom and integer fleet rounding.
  3. Translate the energy difference. At a common grid factor of 0.429 kg/kWh, the NPU-equipped fleet avoids approximately 43.2 t of operational CO2 emissions per year at the stated system boundary.

Decision: Choose the NPU-equipped fleet if the objective is to minimize operational energy under these supplied conditions. Each server draws more power, but its greater useful throughput reduces the required fleet enough to lower joules per completed request. This conclusion depends on meeting the same quality and latency targets; a faster peak arithmetic rate alone would not establish the advantage. A procurement decision must additionally compare acquisition costs, software support, and embodied emissions.

Energy per request completes the selection rule that the lighthouse table began. Hardware selection is not determined by peak speed alone. Energy per useful result, carbon intensity, embodied impact, and total cost of ownership belong beside latency, throughput, and memory capacity, and each is measured against the resource the workload actually exhausts. The misconceptions that follow are the ways teams skip that measurement and choose the wrong hardware path.

Self-Check: Question

  1. On a single H100, which pairing of lighthouse workload and the resource it exhausts first matches the chapter’s lighthouse memory-and-compute comparison?

    1. ResNet-50: memory capacity; GPT-2 XL decode: arithmetic throughput; DLRM: memory bandwidth
    2. ResNet-50: arithmetic throughput once batching amortizes its weights; GPT-2 XL decode: HBM bandwidth; DLRM: memory capacity
    3. ResNet-50: HBM bandwidth; GPT-2 XL decode: memory capacity; DLRM: arithmetic throughput
    4. All three are limited by arithmetic throughput, because the H100’s tensor peak is the binding resource for every workload

  2. In the lifecycle carbon assessment of advanced deep learning accelerators, what constitutes ‘embodied carbon’?

    1. The electrical energy consumed by the GPU during model forward and backward passes
    2. The carbon emitted by datacenter air conditioning units during peak summer load
    3. The carbon credits purchased by cloud providers to offset datacenter energy usage
    4. The greenhouse gas emissions generated during raw material extraction, semiconductor silicon manufacturing, packaging, and hardware transportation

  3. Explain why maximizing useful accelerator utilization can reduce the amortized carbon footprint per completed AI workload, while not automatically reducing total carbon emissions.

11.12 Fallacies and Pitfalls

Hardware acceleration often defies intuition because headline specifications mask workload-specific bottlenecks. The fallacies and pitfalls here capture selection, scaling, and optimization errors that leave expensive compute resources underused. Sound system evaluation follows one diagnostic habit instead: characterize the workload arithmetic intensity, identify the physical bottleneck metric, match execution to the appropriate datapath, and account for interconnect, scaling, and portability costs.

Fallacy: More specialized hardware always provides better performance than general-purpose alternatives.

Specialized accelerators achieve high efficiency only when workload access patterns match underlying execution datapaths: the core tenet of algorithm-machine co-design. On the roofline (section 11.6), the A100 reference tensor path has a ridge point of 153 FLOP/byte; below that ridge, increasing its 312 TFLOP/s arithmetic peak does not raise the modeled bandwidth ceiling. A transformer attention softmax with \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) = 2 FLOP/byte–5 FLOP/byte is capped at 4.1 TFLOP/s–10.2 TFLOP/s (3.3 percent of tensor peak) on an A100. On a CPU, whose ridge point sits around 10 FLOP/byte–20 FLOP/byte, the same traffic model places the kernel below the reference ridge, and its bandwidth ceiling represents 10 percent–50 percent of the CPU’s compute capacity. These fractions are modeled bandwidth bounds, not measured utilization. When workloads have irregular memory access, tiny batch sizes, or dynamic control flow, highly parallel execution pipelines stall on memory latency and thread divergence. General-purpose CPUs with large cache hierarchies, out-of-order execution, and branch predictors often deliver superior latency and resource efficiency under these conditions. Hardware selection requires matching workload arithmetic intensity and dataflow regularity to architectural ridge points rather than assuming specialization guarantees speed.

Pitfall: Ignoring memory bandwidth limitations when selecting acceleration strategies.

Procurement decisions frequently target peak arithmetic throughput while overlooking memory interface constraints. Off-chip data movement imposes severe performance and energy penalties: fetching an operand from DRAM consumes roughly 640 pJ compared to 0.5 pJ for a small, register-adjacent L1 SRAM access, the cheapest tier noted in the caption of figure 4. Consider an accelerator providing 300 TFLOP/s of compute alongside 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth, setting a ridge point of 150 FLOP/byte. A normalization kernel such as LayerNorm with an arithmetic intensity of 1.5 FLOP/byte has a bandwidth ceiling of 3 TFLOP/s (1 percent of compute peak). Under the stated HBM streaming assumption, memory bandwidth supplies this upper bound, and adding compute units alone does not raise it.

Fallacy: Hardware acceleration benefits scale linearly with additional accelerators.

Distributed training need not deliver \(8\times\) throughput on eight accelerators because exposed inter-chip communication can reduce parallel efficiency. Synchronizing gradients across ranks via ring AllReduce makes each rank send and receive about twice the gradient payload (equation 8.12), or 1.75× payloads across eight devices. With an interconnect such as NVLink providing 600 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth (half that per direction), transmitting a 1 GB gradient payload consumes 5.83 ms. For a model with a 50 ms compute step, this data exchange adds 11.7 percent communication overhead before counting software collective latency. Without compute-communication pipelining, an eight-accelerator node reaches only 7.2× speedup (89.6 percent parallel efficiency). Stragglers, barrier synchronizations, and collective protocol overhead widen the gap between linear expectations and physical cluster scaling.

Pitfall: Planning accelerator capacity from peak FLOP/s specifications.

Peak FLOP/s measures arithmetic unit capacity under ideal instruction mixes and continuous operand availability, not delivered application throughput. Realized performance depends on kernel arithmetic intensity, matrix dimensions, memory coalescing, and runtime launch overhead. The roofline model (section 11.6) bounds the gap between peak compute and bandwidth-limited execution. On an A100 GPU with a 312 TFLOP/s peak, an illustrative dense-transformer scenario supplies a sustained range of 120 TFLOP/s–180 TFLOP/s (40 percent–60 percent model FLOPs utilization). This supplied range is illustrative, not a measurement or a prediction for every model. Sizing cluster capacity from peak FLOP/s creates severe under-provisioning; capacity planning must rely on measured sustained throughput or roofline-bounded kernel projections.

Fallacy: One peak FLOP/s rating describes a workload at every precision.

Accelerators have separate datapaths for different precisions, and the peak throughput varies dramatically across them. An H100 delivers roughly 989 TFLOP/s in FP16 tensor operations but only about 67 TFLOP/s in FP32 CUDA-core operations: a roughly 15× gap within the same chip (Choquette 2023). Dividing achieved BF16 model FLOP/s by the smaller FP32 peak inflates the reported utilization, while using that FP32 peak to estimate ideal training time overestimates the time. Matching against the wrong roofline misclassifies kernels as compute-bound when they are memory-bound (or vice versa). Useful model FLOP utilization divides the model’s useful operations per elapsed second by the matching supported precision and execution-path peak. Hardware busy time is a different metric: an active device can spend time on transfers, redundant work, or fallback execution. Quote the denominator and precision explicitly.

Pitfall: Deploying small-batch inference workloads on high-compute accelerators.

Small-batch dense inference can use only a small fraction of arithmetic peak because single-sample execution lacks cross-sample parameter reuse. For a dense linear projection with widths \(\LayerInputWidth=\LayerOutputWidth=2048\), a single request (\(\BatchSize=1\)) is modeled as streaming the entire weight tensor from device memory to execute a matrix-vector product, yielding an arithmetic intensity of only 1 FLOP/byte. At batch size \(\BatchSize=256\), weight reuse amortizes memory transfers across tokens, elevating arithmetic intensity to 204.8 FLOP/byte. At \(\BatchSize=1\), memory bandwidth bounds performance at 2.04 TFLOP/s on an A100 and 0.32 TFLOP/s on a T4. Although the T4 provides a lower peak of 65 TFLOP/s with a ridge point of 203.1 FLOP/byte, the two batch-1 ceilings differ by 6.4×, which is exactly their memory-bandwidth ratio. The A100’s 4.8× advantage in peak compute contributes nothing. The A100 costs 6× as much as the T4, so their modeled batch-1 throughput ceilings per dollar are nearly the same. Actual procurement requires measured latency, throughput, memory fit, and the intended request mix.

Fallacy: Vendor-specific optimizations have no long-term portability cost.

Optimizing exclusively for a single vendor runtime captures immediate kernel efficiency but introduces severe architectural lock-in (section 11.8). Codebases saturated with proprietary device intrinsics, vendor-specific assembly, and non-standard memory layouts require months of engineering labor to port when newer, more cost-effective accelerators emerge. This technical debt delays hardware transitions and prevents multi-vendor procurement. To preserve flexibility, systems must isolate vendor-tuned micro-kernels behind hardware abstraction layers or target intermediate compiler representations (such as Triton or MLIR).

Checkpoint 11.5: Feasibility assessment: Can you run it?

Before procuring hardware, validate each physical constraint. These failure modes translate into a concrete feasibility test:

Self-Check: Question

  1. A team prunes \(70\%\) of the weights in a large language model using unstructured magnitude pruning, setting those weights to zero. However, when executing the pruned model on standard GPU dense Tensor Cores, inference latency is identical to or slower than the unpruned baseline. What is the primary cause of this pitfall?

    1. Standard dense hardware cannot skip arbitrary zero elements efficiently, and compact sparse formats add metadata and irregular access overhead
    2. Floating-point units automatically convert zero values into infinite loops
    3. Unstructured pruning forces the GPU driver to downclock memory bandwidth to prevent overheating
    4. The operating system kernel intercepts every zero multiplication and raises a hardware page fault

  2. Describe the pitfall of ‘micro-offloading’ small tensor operations from CPU to GPU, and explain why a sequence of scalar operations can run slower on an accelerator than on the host CPU.

  3. For the given diagnostic procedure for an underperforming training workload on an already distributed accelerator cluster—broad trace first, then communication check, then exposed-kernel analysis, then intervention—place the following steps in that sequence:

  1. Roofline & Hardware Counter Analysis: Determine whether exposed kernels are compute-bound, memory-bandwidth-bound, or latency-bound
  2. End-to-End Profiling: Identify data loading stalls, host-device synchronization, and the full critical path
  3. Targeted Optimization: Apply the intervention that matches the identified critical bottleneck
  4. Multi-Device Communication Profiling: Inspect collective communication delays and interconnect saturation

  1. Which of the following statements represents a classic fallacy regarding peak accelerator specifications?

    1. Higher memory bandwidth can raise the bandwidth ceiling for some memory-bound workloads
    2. An accelerator with \(2\times\) higher peak theoretical TFLOP/s will automatically deliver a \(2\times\) speedup on any neural network workload
    3. Kernel fusion can improve arithmetic intensity by reducing global memory traffic
    4. Warp divergence reduces the execution efficiency of SIMT processor lanes
